How every stop is built

Each topic follows the same order so you always know where you are:

Prerequisites primer

Big idea

Everything the later chapters quietly assume: how to read the code, how arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues behave, the three bits of maths that appear everywhere (logarithms, sums, powers), and the Python you need. Skim what you know; do the two small labs.

How to read the code in this notebook

All code is Python, chosen because it reads almost like pseudocode. If you have never programmed, these are the only constructs you need.

You seeIt means
a = [5, 2, 9]A list (array) of three numbers. a[0] is 5, a[2] is 9. Indexing starts at 0. len(a) is 3.
a[-1]The last element (counting from the end).
for x in a:Repeat the indented lines once for each element x of a.
for i in range(n):Repeat with i = 0, 1, …, n−1. range(a, b) stops before b. range(n-1, -1, -1) counts down from n−1 to 0.
while cond:Repeat while the condition stays true.
if / elif / elseChoose one branch.
def f(x): return yDefine a function f that gives back y. A function calling itself is recursion.
a, b = b, aSwap two values in one line.
7 // 2 and 7 % 2Integer division (3) and remainder (1). (i - 1) // 2 is how we find a heap parent.
None"Nothing here". An empty child pointer in a tree, or "no value yet".
x ≤ y written as x <= yComparison operators: < <= > >= == !=. Note == compares, = assigns.
arr[:]A copy of the list. Plain b = a does NOT copy; both names point to the same list.

Indentation (the spaces at the start of a line) shows which lines belong inside a loop, an if or a function. Indentation is the "brackets" of Python.

Memory in one page: variables, arrays, linked lists

Think of computer memory as a very long row of numbered boxes. A variable is a labelled box. Two ways of storing a collection of items:

Array (Python list)

Items sit in consecutive boxes. Because the boxes are side by side, the computer finds item number i by simple arithmetic: O(1) access by index. Inserting or deleting in the middle forces everything after it to shift: O(n). Appending to the end is O(1) (amortised).

Linked list

Each item is a small node holding a value and a pointer (the address) of the next node. Nodes can be anywhere in memory. Reaching item i means following i pointers: O(n). But inserting right after a node you already hold is O(1): just rewire two pointers.

Remember

A pointer (reference) is just "where to find another node". A tree node holds two pointers (left and right); a graph vertex holds a list of them. None means "no node there". This idea powers chapters 4 to 8.

Stack: last in, first out (LIFO)

A stack of plates: you put a plate on top and take the top one off. The last plate added is the first removed. Three operations, all O(1): push (add to top), pop (remove and return top), peek (look at top).

Where you will meet it: the recursion call stack (each active function call is a plate), DFS, undo buttons, matching brackets.

Queue: first in, first out (FIFO)

A line at a ticket counter: people join at the back and leave from the front. The first to arrive is the first served. Operations: enqueue (join at back), dequeue (leave from front), both O(1).

Where you will meet it: BFS, level-order tree traversal, scheduling.

Sets and dictionaries (hashing)

A set remembers which items it has seen. A dictionary maps a key to a value (name → phone number). Both answer "is this key present?" in about O(1) time on average, thanks to hashing (the key is turned into a position in a table). You will use a set or boolean array for visited and a dictionary for memo.

Trees at a glance

A tree stores hierarchical data: a folder containing folders, a family tree, a company chart. There is one top node, the root; every other node hangs below exactly one parent; nodes with nothing below are leaves. Chapter 4 builds this up carefully, from the rules to every operation.

Maths you need: powers, logarithms, sums

Powers of 2

Computing uses 2 constantly. Learn these: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 ≈ 10³ (a thousand), 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ (a million), 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹ (a billion).

The logarithm: "how many times can I halve it?"

log₂ n (written lg n, or just log n in this course) is the answer to: how many times can I cut n in half before I reach 1? Equivalently, it is the power you raise 2 to in order to get n: 210 = 1024, so log₂ 1024 = 10.

n8161,0001,000,0001,000,000,000
log₂ n (about)34102030

This is why log n algorithms are astonishingly fast: a billion items need only about 30 steps. Binary search, balanced trees and heaps all get their speed from halving the problem each step, or from a tree whose height is log n.

Remember

Log rules you will use: log(a·b) = log a + log b. log(n²) = 2·log n. Changing the base only changes a constant: log₂n = log₁₀n / log₁₀2, so in Big-O we never write the base. And log_b(a) in the Master theorem means "the power of b that gives a"; for example log₃ 27 = 3 because 3³ = 27.

Floor and ceiling

⌊x⌋ rounds down (⌊3.7⌋ = 3). ⌈x⌉ rounds up (⌈3.2⌉ = 4). Heap parents use ⌊(i−1)/2⌋; a tree with n nodes needs a height of at least ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ − 1.

Factorial

n! = n × (n−1) × … × 2 × 1, with 0! = 1. It counts the ways to arrange n distinct items: 3! = 6, 5! = 120, 10! = 3,628,800.

Sums you need to recognise

SumValueWhy it matters
1 + 2 + 3 + … + nn(n+1)/2Triangular loops, Quick Sort worst case: O(n²)
1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2k2k+1 − 1Levels of a tree: the last level is about half of all nodes
1 + ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + …never reaches 2 (< 2)A shrinking series: the first term dominates
1 + ½ + ⅓ + … + 1/nabout ln nQuick Sort average-case analysis
Teacher's note

Why n(n+1)/2? Write the numbers forwards and backwards and add column by column: (1+n) + (2+(n−1)) + … Each of the n columns sums to n+1, and we counted everything twice, so the total is n(n+1)/2. Pair the first with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on.

Symbols

Σ"sum of"∈"is an element of"
∃"there exists"∀"for all"
≈"approximately"→"tends to" / "leads to" / edge direction
lglog base 2εa tiny positive number
V, Enumber of vertices / edgeshheight of a tree

Exam trap

Creating a 2D grid: [[0]*n]*n is a classic bug. It makes n references to the same row. Use [[0]*n for _ in range(n)] to get n separate rows.

Tracing code by hand

Big idea

Before you can design an algorithm you have to be able to run one in your head. A trace table records every variable after every step; a call stack records every function call that hasn't finished yet. Both are exactly what "dry run" questions ask for, and stop 1 starts writing recursive code straight away.

The trace table

One column per variable, one row per step (usually one loop iteration). Fill it in strictly in order; never skip ahead to what you "know" the answer is.

Stepia[i]a[i] > best?best after the step
start–––3
118yes8
222no8
339yes9
444no9
return9

Loop invariants: what stays true every lap

A loop invariant is a sentence about the variables that is true every time the loop is about to go round again. For find_max: "best is the largest value in a[0..i]". You check three things, exactly as CLRS does:

CheckQuestionFor find_max
InitialisationIs it true before the first iteration?best = a[0] is the largest of a[0..0].
MaintenanceIf it is true before an iteration, is it still true after?If a[i] beats the old maximum it becomes best; otherwise best stays the largest.
TerminationWhen the loop stops, what does it tell you?i reached n − 1, so best is the largest of the whole array.
Teacher's note

Invariants are how the rest of the course explains its algorithms. Quick Sort's partition keeps "everything in a[lo..k] is ≤ pivot". Sift down keeps "the heap rule holds everywhere except at i". BFS keeps "the queue holds vertices in order of distance". When an explanation in a later stop says "at every step…", it is stating an invariant.

Tracing recursion: frames and the way back

Every call gets its own frame: its own copy of the parameters and local variables. When a function calls itself, the caller pauses on that line and waits. The lines after the call run later, on the way back, once the inner call returns. Research on how students learn recursion finds that this "backward flow" is one of the most common sticking points, so trace it deliberately.

EventCall stack (top on the right)What happens
calli=0i ≠ 3, call total(a, 1) and pause
calli=0 · i=1call total(a, 2) and pause
calli=0 · i=1 · i=2call total(a, 3) and pause
calli=0 · i=1 · i=2 · i=3base case: return 0
returni=0 · i=1 · i=2rest = 0, return 5 + 0 = 5
returni=0 · i=1rest = 5, return 1 + 5 = 6
returni=0rest = 6, return 4 + 6 = 10

The deepest moment has n + 1 frames on the stack, which is why recursion over n items costs O(n) space even when it allocates nothing else.

Exam trap

Each frame has its own variables: the i in one call is not the i in another. And a recursive function whose base case is missing or unreachable doesn't loop forever quietly: Python stops it with RecursionError after about 1,000 nested calls (the default limit).

Remember
  • Trace table: one column per variable, one row per step, filled strictly in order.
  • Invariant: true before the loop, kept by every lap, useful when the loop ends.
  • Recursion: one frame per call; the caller pauses; code after the call runs on the way back.
  • Deepest stack = space cost of the recursion.

Foundations line

Problem-solving foundations

Big idea

Before any data structure: how to read a problem, choose a strategy, and know whether your idea is fast enough before you write a line of code.

What is an algorithm, really?

An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous list of steps that turns an input into a desired output. A recipe is an algorithm for cooking. "Look up a word by opening the dictionary in the middle, deciding which half the word is in, and repeating" is an algorithm for searching.

A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that certain operations are cheap. Arrays make "get the 5th item" cheap. Heaps make "get the biggest item" cheap. Trees make "find this key" cheap. Every algorithm in this course is really a pairing: a data structure plus a strategy for using it.

Teacher's note

When you meet any new topic in this course, ask three questions in order: (1) What rule does this structure enforce? (2) Which operations does that rule make fast? (3) What does keeping the rule cost on insert and delete? Every chapter below is organised around those three questions.

A repeatable approach for any problem

Exam questions and interview questions both reward a calm routine over inspiration. Use these six steps.

StepWhat you doTypical mistake it prevents
1. UnderstandRestate the problem. Write the input, the output, and the limits (how big can n be? can values repeat? can the input be empty?). Make one small example by hand.Solving a different problem from the one asked.
2. Brute forceDescribe the slowest correct solution, even if silly. State its time complexity.Having no answer at all. Also gives you a correctness checker.
3. Match a patternLook at the clue words (table below) and choose a technique: sort, heap, BST, BFS, DFS, backtracking, DP.Reinventing something that already has a name.
4. PlanWrite pseudocode or the recurrence on paper. Decide the data structures.Starting to code and getting lost halfway.
5. Dry runTrace your plan on the example by hand, then on edge cases: empty, one element, duplicates, already sorted, all equal, maximum size.Off-by-one errors and missed base cases.
6. AnalyseState time and space complexity, and compare with the limit from step 1.Submitting something that is correct but too slow.

Let the input size choose your algorithm

A modern computer does roughly 108 simple operations per second. If the problem tells you the largest n, you can work out which complexity classes are allowed before designing anything.

Largest nComplexity you can affordTypical technique
n ≤ 10 or 11O(n!)Try all permutations (backtracking)
n ≤ 20 to 25O(2n)Try all subsets
n ≤ 500O(n³)Triple loops, some DP
n ≤ 5,000O(n²)Double loops, simple DP
n ≤ 106O(n log n)Sorting, heaps, balanced trees
n ≤ 107 to 108O(n)One pass, hashing, BFS/DFS
n larger than thatO(log n) or O(1)Binary search, math formula

Worked example: two numbers that add to a target

Worked example

Problem. Given a list of n numbers and a target T, decide whether two different positions hold numbers that add up to T. Example: [8, 3, 5, 11], T = 14 → yes (3 + 11).

Brute force (step 2). Check every pair. There are n(n−1)/2 pairs, so O(n²) time, O(1) space.

Better idea (step 3). For each number x, the partner we need is T − x. If we remember the numbers already seen in a set, we can ask "have I seen T − x?" in O(1). One pass: O(n) time, O(n) space. We traded memory for speed.

Remember

Almost every optimisation in this course follows the same story: spot the repeated or wasted work in the brute force, then add a structure (set, heap, tree, table) that removes it.

Recursion: the engine behind half of this course

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs three ingredients:

  • Base case: the smallest problem, answered directly. Without it the function never stops.
  • Subproblem: a strictly smaller input (n−1, or half the array, or the left subtree).
  • Recursive call: trust that the call returns the correct answer for the smaller input, then use it to build your answer.

Each call waits on the call stack until the call it made returns. Dry run of factorial(4):

MomentCall stack (bottom → top)What happens
1f(4)4 ≠ 0, so compute 4 × f(3). Wait.
2f(4), f(3)3 × f(2). Wait.
3f(4), f(3), f(2)2 × f(1). Wait.
4f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1)1 × f(0). Wait.
5f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1), f(0)Base case: return 1.
6 (unwinding)f(1) returns 1×1 = 1, f(2) returns 2, f(3) returns 6, f(4) returns 24The stack is popped one frame at a time.
Exam trap

Recursion uses memory. factorial(n) is O(n) time and also O(n) space, because n frames sit on the stack at once. Exam questions about "space complexity of a recursive function" are asking about the stack depth.

Strategy families you will meet

Divide and conquer

Split the input into fractions (like halves), solve each recursively, combine. Merge Sort and Quick Sort. Note: factorial is recursive but not divide and conquer, because it shrinks by 1, not by a fraction.

Complete search / backtracking

Try every possibility, building the answer one choice at a time, and undo choices that fail. Slow in theory, but pruning makes it practical.

Dynamic programming

Like complete search, but remember the answer to each subproblem so it is never computed twice.

Greedy

Take the locally best choice and never look back. Fast, but only correct when the problem has a special structure. (Not in your syllabus list, but useful to contrast with DP.)

Added: missing from your notes

Debugging checklist you can use in the exam. Empty input. Single element. Two elements. Duplicates. Already sorted. Reverse sorted. All equal. Negative numbers. The largest allowed n. If your dry run survives all nine, you are probably right.

Growth, limits and induction

Big idea

Stop 2 compares functions as n grows huge, and proves recurrences with induction. Two tools make that painless: look at the ratio f(n)/g(n) as n grows, and learn the four-line shape of a proof by induction.

Who wins eventually? The ratio test

To compare two running times, divide one by the other and see where the ratio heads as n gets large:

f(n) / g(n) as n growsMeaningExample
→ 0f grows strictly slower: f = O(g) but not Θ(g)100n / n² = 100/n → 0
→ a constant c > 0Same growth: f = Θ(g)(3n² + 5n) / n² → 3
→ ∞f grows strictly faster: f = Ω(g) but not Θ(g)2ⁿ / n¹⁰⁰ → ∞, eventually

This is a shortcut, not the definition. Stop 2 gives the formal version with constants c and n₀; the ratio test tells you quickly which answer to aim for.

The pecking order, and why

Who beats whom (eventually)Why
any power of log n < any power of n(log n)/√n → 0. Even log¹⁰ n loses to n^0.01 in the end.
any power of n < any exponential aⁿ (a > 1)Each +1 to n multiplies aⁿ by a but nᵏ by only (1 + 1/n)ᵏ → 1.
aⁿ < n!n! multiplies by n each step, which eventually exceeds any fixed a.
Exam trap

Log bases don't matter; exponential bases do. log₂ n = 3.32 · log₁₀ n, a constant factor, so both are Θ(log n). But 4ⁿ / 2ⁿ = 2ⁿ → ∞, so 4ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ). Similarly 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2 · 2ⁿ is Θ(2ⁿ), while 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ is not.

Proof by induction in four lines

Induction proves a statement P(n) for every n by knocking over dominoes: show the first one falls, and show that any falling domino knocks over the next.

  1. Claim. State P(n) exactly.
  2. Base. Check P(1) (or P(0)) directly.
  3. Step. Assume P(k) is true for some k (the inductive hypothesis) and use it to show P(k + 1).
  4. Conclude. P(n) holds for all n ≥ the base.
Worked example

Claim: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.
Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1·2/2. ✓
Step: assume 1 + … + k = k(k + 1)/2. Then 1 + … + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, which is the formula for k + 1. ✓
Conclude: true for every n ≥ 1.

The same proof shows the recurrence T(1) = 1, T(n) = T(n − 1) + n solves to n(n + 1)/2: Quick Sort's worst case.

Stop 2's substitution method is exactly this: guess the answer to a recurrence, then prove the guess by induction. If you can do the sum above, you can do that.

Why analyses pretend n is a power of 2

Recurrences like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n only make sense when n/2 is a whole number. Analyses assume n = 2ᵏ so every split is exact; for other n the true cost sits between the costs at the neighbouring powers of 2, which differ by at most a constant factor. The Θ answer doesn't change, so the simplification is safe.

Remember
  • Ratio → 0: slower. → constant: Θ. → ∞: faster.
  • logs < powers < exponentials < factorials. Log bases are constants; exponential bases are not.
  • Induction: claim, base, step (assume k, prove k + 1), conclude.

Complexity analysis

Big idea

Time and space complexity, Big-O and its relatives, best/average/worst case, and how to solve the recurrences that recursive algorithms produce.

Why we count operations, not seconds

The same program runs at different speeds on a laptop and on a phone, in Python and in C. Seconds therefore tell us about the machine. What we want is a property of the algorithm: how does the number of basic operations grow as the input grows?

Teacher's note

Think of two taxi companies. One charges a flat fee however far you go. The other charges per kilometre. For a 1 km trip the flat fee looks bad. For a 100 km trip it wins easily. Complexity analysis is about the 100 km trip: what happens for large n. That is why we ignore small inputs and constant details.

Two rules for simplifying

  1. Drop constant factors. 5n² and n² grow the same way: double n and either one becomes 4× bigger.
  2. Drop smaller terms. In n³ + n² + n, once n is large the n³ part is almost everything.

Applying both rules to a running time gives its order of growth, written with Big-O.

Counting operations in code

The method: find how many times the innermost statement runs. Loops multiply, code in sequence adds (and then the biggest term wins).

Code shapeTimes the body runsComplexity
for i in range(n)nO(n)
for i in range(n): for j in range(n)n × nO(n²)
for i in range(n): for j in range(i)0+1+2+…+(n−1) = n(n−1)/2O(n²)
i = 1; while i < n: i *= 2i takes values 1,2,4,8,… so about log₂n stepsO(log n)
for i in range(n): j = 1; while j < n: j *= 2n × log nO(n log n)
Two separate loops, one after the other (n and n)n + n = 2nO(n)
A loop over n, then a nested n×n loopn + n²O(n²) (bigger term wins)
Naive recursive fib(n) (two calls, each shrinking by 1 or 2)roughly 1.618n callsO(2n) (upper bound)
Exam trap

The triangular loop (for j in range(i)) trips up many students. It is not n log n and it is not "half of n". It sums to n(n−1)/2, which is n²/2 − n/2, and dropping constants and the lower term leaves O(n²).

A recipe for analysing any code

  1. Decide what n is. The size of the input: array length, number of nodes, number of vertices. If there are two inputs (arrays of lengths n and m), keep two variables: a nested loop over both is O(n·m), not O(n²).
  2. Find the basic operation: the line that runs the most (usually the innermost statement or a comparison).
  3. Count how many times it runs as a function of n. Work from the inside out: a loop's count is (iterations) × (cost of its body).
  4. Combine: statements in sequence add; nesting multiplies; an if/else costs the larger branch (for worst case).
  5. Simplify: drop constants and lower-order terms.
RuleExampleResult
Sum ruleO(n) loop followed by O(n²) loopO(n + n²) = O(n²)
Product ruleO(n) loop containing an O(log n) stepO(n log n)
Constants vanish3n + 7O(n)
Two inputs stay separateloop over a (n items) containing loop over b (m items)O(n·m)
Recursion(number of calls) × (work per call)Often needs a recurrence
Hidden costsx in list or slicing inside a loopEach is O(n), so the loop is O(n²)
Worked example

Analyse this.

First loop: n. Second loop nest: n × log n. Sequence adds: n + n log n. The bigger term wins: O(n log n). Space: only a few variables, O(1).

Pick a loop pattern below and watch the real iteration counts as n doubles. The last column is the whole idea of "order of growth": it shows what happens to the work when the input doubles.

The standard ladder of growth rates

From fastest to slowest: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n²) quadratic, O(n³) cubic, O(2ⁿ) exponential, O(n!) factorial. CLRS adds a formal fact: any exponential with base above 1 eventually beats any polynomial (nᵇ = o(aⁿ)), and n! grows faster than 2ⁿ.

Play with the lab below. Slide n and watch how fast the bottom rows leave the others behind.

Asymptotic notation, formally

Your lecture notes use Big-O loosely. CLRS gives five precise symbols. Each describes a set of functions, and "f(n) = O(g(n))" really means "f(n) belongs to that set".

SymbolPlain meaningFormal definitionLike…
O(g)Upper bound: f grows no faster than g∃ c > 0, n₀ such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀≤
Ω(g)Lower bound: f grows at least as fast as g∃ c > 0, n₀ such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n₀≥
Θ(g)Tight bound: both of the above∃ c₁, c₂ > 0, n₀ such that c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀=
o(g)Strictly slower than gf(n)/g(n) → 0 as n → ∞<
ω(g)Strictly faster than gf(n)/g(n) → ∞ as n → ∞>
Remember

Key theorem: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if f(n) = O(g(n)) and f(n) = Ω(g(n)).

Proving it with constants: 3n² + 10n + 5 = O(n²)

We must find c and n₀. Try c = 4. We need 3n² + 10n + 5 ≤ 4n², which rearranges to n² − 10n − 5 ≥ 0. At n = 10 this gives −5 (fails). At n = 11 it gives 6 (works), and it keeps working after that. So c = 4, n₀ = 11 is a valid witness. The lab below lets you hunt for constants yourself.

Exam trap

Big-O is not "worst case". These are two different axes. Which input? (best, average, worst case) is one question. Which bound on the resulting function? (O, Ω, Θ) is another. You can say "the worst-case time of Quick Sort is Θ(n²)" and "the best-case time is Θ(n log n)". Your lecture notes use "Big-O" and "worst case" together as shorthand: "O(n²) means for every input, the time is at most c·n²".

Best, average and worst case

The running time often depends on which input of size n you are given, not just n.

  • Best case: the input that makes the algorithm fastest.
  • Worst case: the input that makes it slowest. This is the usual default, because it is a guarantee.
  • Average case: the expected time over all inputs (needs an assumption about how inputs are distributed).

Linear search for a value in an array shows all three. Try the buttons.

AlgorithmBestAverageWorstWhy the cases differ
Linear searchO(1)O(n)O(n)Target first, middle, or absent
Insertion sortO(n)O(n²)O(n²)Sorted input vs reverse-sorted
Quick Sort (last-element pivot)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n²)Balanced split vs split by 0 and n−1
Merge SortO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)Always halves
BST searchO(1) at the root, usually O(log n)O(log n)O(n)Balanced vs skewed tree

Space complexity

Space complexity counts the extra memory an algorithm needs as n grows. Usually we count auxiliary space: memory beyond the input itself.

  • A few variables: O(1). An in-place swap, a running total.
  • A new array or set of size n: O(n).
  • Recursion: the call stack counts. Depth d means O(d) space. Merge sort needs O(n) for merging; Quick Sort needs O(log n) on average for the stack.

Divide and conquer and recurrences

Divide and conquer has three steps: divide into smaller subproblems of the same kind, conquer by solving them recursively, combine the answers. Merge sort: split the array in half, sort each half, merge. The time is described by a recurrence relation, a one-line equation for a recursive function:

Remember

T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)

a = number of subproblems per call. b = how much the input shrinks. f(n) = work done outside the recursive calls (dividing and combining).

Merge sort: a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n (merging), so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.

Method 1: the recursion tree

Draw every call as a node, write the work at each node, add up each level, then add up the levels. For T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n):

LevelNodesWork per nodeWork in the whole level
01f(n)f(n)
1af(n/b)a·f(n/b)
2a²f(n/b²)a²·f(n/b²)
last: logbnalog_b n = nlog_b af(1) = constantnlog_b a

The tree has about logbn levels. The total depends on how the level sums change as you go down, and there are only three patterns:

Growing

1 + 2 + 4 + … + n. The last term dominates. Total ≈ the last level.

Equal

n + n + … + n over log n levels. Total = one level × number of levels = n log n.

Shrinking

n² + n²/2 + n²/4 + …. The first term dominates. Total ≈ the root.

Worked example

T(n) = 3T(n/4) + cn² (CLRS). Level i has 3i nodes, each costing c(n/4i)², so the level costs (3/16)i·cn². Ratio 3/16 < 1, so the sum shrinks like a geometric series: total ≤ cn²·(1 / (1 − 3/16)) = (16/13)cn². Root dominates, T(n) = Θ(n²).

Unbalanced split T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + cn. Every level costs at most cn. The longest path shrinks by 2/3 each step, so its length is log3/2n. Total = O(n log n). This is why Quick Sort stays fast even with uneven splits.

Method 2: the Master theorem (the cookbook)

For T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1, compute the watershed function nc where c = logba (this is the number of leaves). Then compare f(n) with nc. Whoever is bigger "wins".

CaseComparisonPictureAnswer
1. Leaf heavyf(n) is polynomially smaller than nc: f(n) = O(nc−ε)Bottom level dominatesT(n) = Θ(nc)
2. Balancedf(n) = Θ(nc)Every level equalT(n) = Θ(nc log n)
3. Root heavyf(n) is polynomially larger: f(n) = Ω(nc+ε), and a·f(n/b) ≤ k·f(n) for some k < 1 (regularity)Top level dominatesT(n) = Θ(f(n))
Added: missing from your notes

Two details your slide notes skip. (1) "Smaller" and "larger" must be polynomially so, by a factor of nε for some ε > 0. (2) Case 3 needs the regularity condition. Polynomials like n² always satisfy it. The famous gap: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. Here c = 1 and f(n) = n log n is larger than n, but only by a log n factor, which is smaller than nε for every ε > 0. The theorem does not apply. Use a recursion tree: log n levels each costing about n log n, so the answer is Θ(n log² n).

Use the calculator, then try the practice problems underneath. Predict the case before you press the button.

T(n) = T(n−1) + n (Quick Sort worst case)

Not of the form T(n/b), so the Master theorem does not apply. Unroll: n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2 → Θ(n²).

Method 3: substitution (guess and prove)

Guess the answer, then prove it by induction. Example: T(n) = 2T(⌊n/2⌋) + n, guess T(n) ≤ c·n lg n. Assume it holds for smaller values:

T(n) ≤ 2·c⌊n/2⌋·lg⌊n/2⌋ + n ≤ c·n·lg(n/2) + n = c·n·lg n − c·n + n ≤ c·n·lg n, as long as c ≥ 1.

Added: missing from your notes

Trick when the induction almost works. If proving T(n) ≤ cn + d fails, strengthen the guess by subtracting a lower-order term: try T(n) ≤ cn − d. A stronger hypothesis gives you more to work with in the inductive step.

Amortised analysis, in one paragraph

Added: missing from your notes

A Python list.append is "O(1) amortised". Occasionally the array is full and must be copied to double its size, costing O(n). But that expensive copy happens only after n cheap appends, so spread over all appends the average cost per append is O(1). Amortised means average over a sequence of operations, with no randomness involved. It also explains why building a heap with n inserts costs O(n log n) but the cleverer build-heap costs O(n).

Bridge to stop 3

Array surgery: swaps, pointers and partitions

Big idea

Quick Sort is one idea, partition, applied recursively. Partition is a pattern you can learn on easier problems first: one pointer reads every element once while a second pointer marks the end of the kept zone, and items that pass a test are swapped into it. Learn the pattern here and Lomuto partition will look familiar.

The swap, and why "in place" matters

a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i] exchanges two slots in O(1). An algorithm is in place when it rearranges the input using only O(1) extra memory (a few variables), instead of building new lists. Merge sort builds new lists (O(n) extra); Quick Sort and heap sort only swap.

Two pointers from opposite ends

Start one pointer at each end and walk them towards each other. Each step does O(1) work and moves at least one pointer, so the whole thing is O(n).

Compare stop 1's set-based pair sum: O(n) time but O(n) space. When the input is already sorted, two pointers get the same time with no extra memory.

A reader and a writer: partition by a rule

Move every even number to the front:

At every moment the array is split into three zones. This is the invariant (bridge 0.5):

a[0..k]a[k+1..pos−1]a[pos..]
passed the test (even)failed the test (odd)not read yet

Now replace "is even" with "is ≤ pivot", leave the last element (the pivot) out of the scan, and swap it into slot k + 1 at the end. That is Lomuto partition, line for line:

evens_firstLomuto partition (stop 3)
Testa[pos] % 2 == 0arr[pos] <= pivot
Range scannedwhole arraylo .. hi − 1 (the pivot sits at hi)
After the loopnothingswap the pivot into k + 1, return k + 1
Exam trap

This kind of partition is not stable: evens_first([1, 3, 2]) gives [2, 3, 1], so the odd numbers 1 and 3 swapped order. That is exactly why Quick Sort is not stable.

Three zones: the Dutch national flag

Stop 3 shows that an array of equal values is Quick Sort's worst case: every element goes to the "≤" side. The fix is to split into three zones, less / equal / greater, so all the equal values are finished in one pass.

Teacher's note

The three-way version goes slightly past your syllabus, but it is the clearest way to see why duplicates hurt two-way Quick Sort, and it is a favourite "improve this algorithm" question.

Remember
  • In place = O(1) extra memory, just swaps.
  • Two pointers from both ends: O(n), needs a reason to move one pointer each step (often sortedness).
  • Reader–writer partition: k marks the end of the kept zone; grow k, then swap. Lomuto is this with test "≤ pivot".
  • These partitions are not stable.
3
Sorting and trees line

Advanced sorting: Quick Sort

Big idea

The sort that skips the merge step. Learn partition until you can do it with your eyes closed; everything else follows from it.

Sorting basics (read this first)

Sorting means rearranging a list into increasing (or decreasing) order. It is the most studied problem in computing because so many other tasks, like searching and merging, become easy once data is sorted.

Vocabulary

TermMeaning
Comparison sortLearns the order only by comparing pairs ("is a[i] ≤ a[j]?"). All sorts in this course are comparison sorts.
In-placeUses only O(1) extra memory beyond the array (swapping elements inside it). Quick Sort, heap sort, insertion sort are in-place. Merge sort is not.
StableEqual keys keep their original relative order. Matters when sorting records, e.g. sorting students by grade after sorting them by name. Merge and insertion sort are stable; Quick Sort and heap sort are not.
PivotThe element Quick Sort uses to split the array.
PartitionRearranging so everything ≤ pivot comes before it and everything > pivot after it.

The sorts you already know, in 30 seconds each

SortIdeaTime (worst)Space
BubbleRepeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; big values "bubble" to the end.O(n²)O(1)
SelectionFind the minimum of the unsorted part, swap it to the front. Repeat.O(n²)O(1)
InsertionTake the next element and slide it left into place among the already-sorted prefix (like sorting a hand of cards).O(n²), best O(n)O(1)
MergeSplit in half, sort each half recursively, merge the two sorted halves.O(n log n)O(n)

The quadratic sorts are fine for tiny inputs but hopeless for a million items (10¹² steps). To see exactly what Merge Sort's merge step is (the thing Quick Sort wants to avoid), here it is:

Added: missing from your notes

Why O(n log n) is the best a comparison sort can do. With n distinct items there are n! possible orderings. Each comparison has two outcomes, so after k comparisons you can distinguish at most 2k orderings. To be able to tell all n! orderings apart you need 2k ≥ n!, so k ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n). No comparison-based sort can beat n log n in the worst case, so Merge Sort, Heap Sort and Quick Sort's average are all optimal up to constants.

The motivation

You already know sorts that cost O(n²) (bubble, insertion, selection) and Merge Sort at O(n log n). Merge Sort has one annoying cost: to merge two sorted halves it copies them into extra arrays, so it needs O(n) extra memory.

Quick Sort asks: can we split the array so that no merging is needed at all? Yes, if we split it so that everything in the left part is ≤ everything in the right part. Then sorting the left part and the right part separately automatically sorts the whole array. The work moves from the "combine" step (Merge Sort) to the "divide" step (Quick Sort).

Teacher's note

Picture 20 students who must line up by height. Pick one student as the pivot. Everyone shorter stands on the pivot's left, everyone taller on the right. The pivot is now standing in exactly the right place and never needs to move again. Now repeat inside the left group and inside the right group. When every group has one student, the whole line is sorted.

The rules

  1. Pick a pivot. In your course: the last element.
  2. Partition: rearrange so that all elements ≤ pivot come first, then the pivot, then all elements > pivot.
  3. The pivot is now in its final sorted position. Never touched again.
  4. Recurse on the left part and the right part.
  5. Base case: a part with 0 or 1 element is already sorted.

Partition, step by step

The naive way builds two new lists, smaller[] and greater[], using O(n) extra space (no better than Merge Sort). The in-place way (called Lomuto partition) uses two markers:

  • pos: the scanner. It walks from the left end to just before the pivot.
  • k: the boundary of the "≤ pivot" zone. It starts at lo−1 (the zone is empty) and always points at the last element of the zone.

For each element at pos: if it is ≤ pivot, grow the zone (k += 1) and swap it into the zone. If it is bigger, leave it alone: it automatically becomes part of the "> pivot" zone sitting between k and pos. At the end, swap the pivot into position k+1, right between the two zones.

Dry run of the first partition

Array: [7, 4, 10, 1, 9, 6, 3, 8, 2, 5], lo = 0, hi = 9, pivot = 5, k = −1.

The whole sort, partition by partition

Quick Sort is just partition applied again and again to ever smaller ranges. For the same array, each row is one call that does real work (single elements and empty ranges need no work):

DepthRange (lo..hi)PivotPivot lands atArray afterwards
00..95index 44 1 3 2 5 6 10 8 7 9

The recursion tree has depth 3 here because the splits were reasonably even. The bold entries are values that have arrived at their final position, one per partition. Every element is eventually a pivot or a single-element range, so it ends up in place. Now run it yourself:

How fast is it?

Worst case: Θ(n²)

If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, partition splits n elements into 0 and n−1. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(n), which unrolls to n + (n−1) + … + 1 = Θ(n²). With the last-element pivot, this happens on already sorted or reverse sorted input: the pivot is the maximum every time. It also happens when all elements are equal (every element is ≤ pivot, so k runs all the way to hi−1).

Best case: Θ(n log n)

If the pivot is always the median, each side gets n/2. Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), the same as Merge Sort → Θ(n log n) by Master theorem case 2.

Average case: Θ(n log n)

You do not need a perfect split. Any split in constant proportion keeps the tree logarithmic. Take a terrible 1 : 9 split: T(n) = T(n/10) + T(9n/10) + cn. The deepest path shrinks by a factor of 9/10 each step, so its length is log10/9n = O(log n). Every level costs at most cn. Total ≤ cn × O(log n) = O(n log n). Only splits like 0 : n−1 (constant difference, not proportion) are fatal.

Added: missing from your notes

The formal argument (CLRS 7.4). The running time is dominated by the number of comparisons. Let the elements in sorted order be z₁ … zₙ. Two elements zᵢ and zⱼ are compared at most once, and only if one of them is the first pivot chosen from the range {zᵢ, …, zⱼ}. With a random pivot that happens with probability 2/(j−i+1). Summing: Σᵢ Σⱼ 2/(j−i+1) = O(n log n), because the inner sum is a harmonic series.

Space and the stack

Partition is in-place (O(1)). But the recursion uses a stack: average depth O(log n), worst depth O(n) (the skewed case). A neat fix, not in your notes: after partitioning, recurse into the smaller side and loop on the larger side. The stack is then at most log n deep even in the worst case.

Randomized Quick Sort

An adversary (or just sorted data, which is very common) can feed the last-element rule its worst case. The cure: choose the pivot at random. Either swap a random element into the last position before partitioning, or shuffle the whole array first. No fixed input is bad any more; the expected time is Θ(n log n) for every input. The worst case still exists, but its probability is astronomically small.

Added: missing from your notes

Extras examiners like.

  • Pivot strategies: first, last, random, median-of-three (median of first, middle, last).
  • Not stable: equal elements can be reordered by the swaps. Merge Sort is stable.
  • In place (apart from the stack), unlike Merge Sort.
  • Many duplicates: this partition degrades to O(n²) on all-equal input. The fix is 3-way partition (less / equal / greater), used by real libraries.
  • Hoare partition is the older two-pointer scheme (pointers move inward from both ends); it does fewer swaps. What you have learned is the Lomuto scheme.
  • Quickselect: to find the k-th smallest element, partition once and recurse into only the side containing position k. Average O(n).

Exam trap

"Quick Sort is O(n log n)" is only the average claim. If a question says "worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort", the answer is O(n²). If it says "on a sorted array with the last element as pivot", the answer is also O(n²).

Patterns for contests: sorting

Seen in your contests

Contest 1 Q5 asked for Quick Sort in descending order and scored by test. The usual trap: with the last element as pivot, a reverse-sorted or all-equal array makes every partition peel off a single element. That is n² work and n levels of recursion. The fix is a random pivot, a three-way split so equal values are finished at once, and an explicit stack.

PatternWords in the statementTool
Sort, then scan“overlapping”, “closest”, “group equal”, “pair up”sort, then one pass
Custom order“arrange to make the largest number”, “order by two rules”key= or cmp_to_key
k-th without sorting“median”, “k-th largest”, n largequickselect, expected O(n); or a heap
Count out-of-order pairs“number of swaps”, “pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]”merge sort that counts while merging
Small value rangevalues up to 10⁶, “frequencies”counting sort, Counter
Minimise the maximum“smallest x such that …”sort, then binary search the answer (stop 14)

In a contest, use Python’s built-in sort (stable, O(n log n)). Write Quick Sort yourself only when the problem tells you to.

Quickselect is Quick Sort that follows only one side: after the split, the answer lies in exactly one of the three zones.

The merge step is the only place that changes: when an element of the right half is placed before the remaining left elements, it jumps over every one of them, and each jump is one inversion.

Exam traps

a.sort() returns None (use sorted(a) to keep the original). A comparison function needs cmp_to_key. Touching intervals [1,4] and [4,5] merge when the statement says “overlap or touch” and not when it says “share a point”. Lomuto partition with the last element as pivot is O(n²) on sorted input: say so in a written answer.

Remember

Sort first and the problem often becomes one pass. Out-of-order pairs: count while merging.

A fixed pivot loses to sorted input; a random pivot and a three-way split don’t.

Names, references and linked structures

Big idea

In Python a variable is a name tag tied to an object, not a box holding it. Trees are objects pointing at objects. Every BST operation in stop 4 relies on one habit: a function that might replace a subtree returns the new subtree, and the caller re-attaches it.

Names are tags, not boxes

Kind of statementExampleEffect on other names for the same object
Mutate the objectb.append(3), b[0] = 9, node.left = xVisible through every name
Rebind the nameb = [0], b = b + [4], node = Node(5)Only this name moves; others are untouched

Studies of students learning Python keep finding that a shaky picture of references causes later confusion, so it is worth getting this exactly right now.

Passing to a function works the same way

A parameter is just a new name for the caller's object. Mutating it is visible to the caller; rebinding it is not.

When node is None there is no object to mutate, so the new node can only reach the tree if the function returns it and the caller writes parent.left = insert(parent.left, value).

Linked lists: the training ground for trees

A linked-list node has one pointer (next); a tree node has two (left, right). Every pattern you need for trees appears first on lists.

QuestionOn a listOn a binary tree (stop 4)
How many nodes?0 if h is None else 1 + length(h.next)0 if n is None else 1 + size(n.left) + size(n.right)
Find a valuewalk next until found: O(n)go left or right each step: O(h)
Delete a nodereturn head.next to skip itreturn a child (or a successor) to replace it
Exam traps

b = a does not copy a list; use a[:] or list(a). In reverse, overwriting cur.next before saving it loses the rest of the list. In any recursive structure, calling delete(head.next, x) without assigning the result back silently changes nothing.

Remember
  • Mutating an object is seen through every name; rebinding a name is not.
  • A function that may replace the head or a subtree must return it, and the caller re-attaches it.
  • Lists are trees with one child: recursion on them has the same shape.

Sorting and trees line

Binary trees and Binary Search Trees

Big idea

Binary search brings an "ignore half the data" trick to dynamic data. Learn the one rule, and search, insert and delete all follow.

Binary trees from scratch

Why trees at all?

An array or list is linear: items are in a single row, so finding something means walking along it. Real data is often hierarchical: a folder holds folders, a company has managers and reports, a decision leads to further decisions. A tree stores that shape directly, and (as the next chapters show) a well-shaped tree lets you reach any item in about log n steps instead of n.

Definition

Remember

A binary tree is either empty, or a root node together with a left subtree and a right subtree, each of which is itself a binary tree.

That definition is recursive, and this is not an accident: almost every tree algorithm is a recursive function that handles "the empty tree" (base case) and "the root plus two smaller trees" (recursive case).

The rules of a binary tree

  1. One root. There is exactly one topmost node, and it has no parent. (A tree may be empty.)
  2. One parent each. Every other node has exactly one parent: the node directly above it.
  3. At most two children, and they are labelled. A node has a left child and/or a right child, each possibly missing. "Only a left child" and "only a right child" are different trees.
  4. No cycles, and connected. From the root there is exactly one path down to every node. You can never walk around in a loop.
  5. No rule about the values. A plain binary tree may hold any values in any arrangement. Extra ordering rules are what make a BST (this chapter) or a heap (next chapter).
Exam trap

Students often mix up the rules. "Parent greater than child" is the heap rule. "Left smaller than node, right larger" is the BST rule. A plain binary tree has neither. Keep the three apart: shape rules (at most 2 children; complete) and value rules (BST order; heap order).

What a node looks like in code

A leaf is a node whose left and right are both None. The whole tree is referred to by a single variable: the root. If you hold the root you can reach everything.

Counting facts you can quote in an exam

FactWhy it is true
A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges.Every node except the root has exactly one edge going up to its parent.
Level i (root = level 0) holds at most 2i nodes.Each node can have at most 2 children, so every level can at most double the one above.
A tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes.1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2h (a geometric sum). Example: height 2 → 7 nodes.
A tree with n nodes has height at least ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ − 1, and at most n − 1.Best case: levels packed full. Worst case: a single chain.
A full binary tree has leaves = internal nodes + 1.Count edges both ways: n − 1 = 2 × (internal nodes), with n = internal + leaves.
A binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 empty (None) child slots.2n slots in total, and n − 1 of them are used by edges.

The heart of the whole chapter: height controls speed. A packed tree of a million nodes has height about 20, so a path from the root to anywhere is about 20 steps. A chain of a million nodes has height 999,999. Same nodes, wildly different performance.

Shapes of binary trees

Two ways to store a binary tree

Pointer nodes

Each node is an object with left and right pointers (as above). Works for any shape. Used for BSTs.

Array

Store level by level; the children of index i live at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent at (i − 1) // 2. No pointers needed, but gaps would waste space, so it is used only for complete trees, which is exactly what heaps are.

Three small recursive helpers

Every tree function follows one pattern: handle None, then combine the answers for the left and right subtrees. Learn this and the rest of the chapter becomes easy.

Terminology cheat sheet

A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges, with no cycles. A binary tree is a tree where each node has at most two children, called left and right. Each node stores a value and two pointers.

TermMeaning
RootThe top node, which has no parent.
LeafA node with no children.
Parent / child / siblingRelationships along edges.
SubtreeA node together with all its descendants.
Depth of a nodeNumber of edges from the root to that node. Root has depth 0.
Height of a treeNumber of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. (Empty tree: −1 by CLRS, 0 in some books. State your convention.)
Full / Perfect / CompleteFull: every node has 0 or 2 children. Perfect: all leaves at the same depth, all levels full. Complete: all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled left to right (heaps use this).

The three depth-first traversals

A traversal visits every node once. The three classic orders differ only in when you handle the node relative to its subtrees. A handy mnemonic: the name says where the node goes.

TraversalOrderResult
Preordernode, left, right1 2 4 7 3 6
Inorderleft, node, right4 2 7 1 3 6
Postorderleft, right, node4 7 2 6 3 1
Level order (BFS)row by row1 2 3 4 7 6
Remember

Traversals are all forms of DFS (go deep, then backtrack). Level order is BFS. You will meet both again on graphs in chapter 8.

How to carry out a traversal by hand

Each rule is the same recursive recipe with the "visit the node" step placed at a different moment:

  • Preorder (NLR): visit the node, then do the left subtree, then the right subtree.
  • Inorder (LNR): do the left subtree, then visit the node, then the right subtree.
  • Postorder (LRN): do the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the node.
Teacher's note

The flag trick. Walk once around the outside of the tree, starting at the left of the root and keeping the tree on your left. Preorder writes a node when you pass its left side (first time you meet it). Inorder writes it when you pass underneath it. Postorder writes it when you pass its right side (the last time you see it).

Edit the tree below (level order, # for a missing child) and step through each traversal. Watch the call stack: every pending call is a node still waiting for its subtrees to finish. When a call hits None it returns at once; that is the base case.

The BST rule

Remember

For every node x: all values in x's left subtree are smaller than x, and all values in x's right subtree are larger than x. The rule must hold at every node, not just the root.

  • Duplicates: either forbid them, or always send them the same way (say, right). Never mix. (CLRS writes left ≤ node ≤ right; your notes use strict < and >. Say which convention you use.)
  • Why it helps: at a node, one comparison tells you which entire half of the remaining tree can be ignored. This is binary search, but on a linked structure that supports cheap inserts and deletes (unlike a sorted array, where insert is O(n) because of shifting).
  • Superpower: an inorder traversal of a BST prints keys in sorted order in Θ(n). Because left < node < right is exactly the inorder visit order.
Exam trap

A tree where each node is merely bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child is not necessarily a BST. Example: root 10, left child 5, and 5's right child 15. Locally fine (15 > 5), but 15 is in the left subtree of 10 and must be less than 10. We come back to this in "validate a BST" below.

The BST rules, stated precisely

  1. A BST is a binary tree (at most two children per node).
  2. For every node x: every key in x's left subtree is smaller than x's key, and every key in x's right subtree is larger.
  3. The rule is recursive: x's left and right subtrees are themselves BSTs.
  4. Decide one duplicate policy: reject duplicates, or always send an equal key to the same side.

Operations

Search

Start at the root. If the target is smaller, go left; larger, go right; equal, found; fell off the tree (None), not present. Each step discards a whole subtree.

Insert

Walk exactly as in search until you reach an empty spot. Put the new node there. A new key always becomes a leaf.

Exam trap

The line node.left = insert(node.left, value) must assign the return value. If you write just insert(node.left, value), the new node is created but never linked to its parent and is lost.

Minimum, maximum, successor

  • Minimum: keep going left until there is no left child. Maximum: keep going right.
  • Inorder successor of x (the next larger key): if x has a right subtree, it is the minimum of that subtree. Otherwise climb up until you arrive from a left child; that ancestor is the successor.

Delete: the three cases

This is the operation examiners love. Find the node z, then look at how many children it has.

CaseWhat to doWhy it is safe
1. Leaf (no children)Remove it (set the parent's pointer to None).Nothing hangs below it.
2. One childReplace z by its only child (the parent now points to that child).The whole child subtree was on the correct side of the parent, so it stays valid.
3. Two childrenFind z's inorder successor y = minimum of z's right subtree. Copy y's value into z. Then delete y from the right subtree (y has no left child, so that is case 1 or 2).y is the smallest key larger than z, so it is greater than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right. (Symmetric alternative: use the predecessor, the maximum of the left subtree.)
Added: missing from your notes

CLRS's version does not copy values; it relinks nodes with a helper called TRANSPLANT(u, v) that replaces the subtree rooted at u by the subtree rooted at v. Case 3 there: if the successor y is z's right child, replace z by y directly; otherwise first replace y by y's right child, then replace z by y. Copying values (above) is simpler to write; relinking is better when other code holds pointers to nodes.

Worked trace: build, then delete

Worked example

Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in that order. 50 becomes the root. 30 < 50 → left. 70 → right. 20 → left of 50, then left of 30. 40 → left of 50, right of 30. 60 → right of 50, left of 70. 80 → right of 70. A perfectly balanced tree of height 2; inorder gives 20 30 40 50 60 70 80.

Delete 50 (root, two children): successor = minimum of the right subtree = 60. Copy 60 into the root, then delete the original 60 (a leaf). Inorder now: 20 30 40 60 70 80. Delete 30 next (two children 20 and 40): successor = 40 (minimum of its right subtree). Copy, remove old 40. Try it on the lab.

Cost: it all depends on the height h

Search, insert, delete, min, max, successor all follow a single root-to-leaf path, so each costs O(h).

Tree shapeHeightEach operationHow it happens
Balanced≈ log₂nO(log n)Keys arrive in a mixed order
Randomly builtexpected O(log n)expected O(log n)Random insertion order (CLRS 12.4: same analysis as Quick Sort)
Skewedn − 1O(n)Keys inserted in sorted order, producing a "linked list"
Exam trap

A plain BST is not self-balancing. "BST operations are O(log n)" is only true for balanced trees. Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order in the lab and watch it collapse into a line.

Added: missing from your notes

Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) fix this: after each insert or delete they use rotations to keep the height O(log n) always, so worst-case operations are O(log n). AVL keeps the heights of the left and right subtrees of every node within 1 of each other. Not needed for this exam beyond knowing why they exist.

Problem solving with BSTs

Almost every BST problem uses one of three ideas: (a) inorder = sorted; (b) use the rule to discard half the tree; (c) pass down bounds that every node in a subtree must respect.

1. Validate a BST

Passing bounds down is the key. Each node must lie strictly between the largest ancestor you turned right at and the smallest ancestor you turned left at.

2. k-th smallest element

Inorder visits keys in increasing order, so stop at the k-th visit. O(h + k).

3. Lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two keys

If both keys are smaller than the current node, the LCA is on the left; if both larger, on the right; otherwise the current node is where they split, so it is the LCA. O(h).

4. Sorted array to balanced BST

Take the middle element as the root so both sides have nearly equal size, then recurse on each half. Height = O(log n).

5. Range sum: add all keys between L and R

Prune: if a node is below L, its whole left subtree is too small, so skip it. Likewise above R.

Added: missing from your notes

More patterns to know: floor and ceiling of a key (walk like search and remember the last candidate), convert BST to a sorted linked list (inorder), count nodes in range, two-sum in a BST (inorder to array, then two pointers), recover a BST with two swapped nodes (inorder shows two inversions), find height, check if two trees are identical.

Seen in your contests

Contest 1: Q1 minimum in a BST (keep going left), Q6 balanced BST from a binary tree (inorder gives sorted values, then pick the middle), and Q4 Validate BST (40/80, solved after the deadline). The classic trap there: checking only “left child < node < right child” passes the samples and fails the tests, because a node deep in the right subtree must still be larger than the root. Mid-sem Q1 was a plain inorder traversal.

Try the tree 5 → (left 1, right 6 → (left 3, right 7)). is_bst_wrong says True; is_bst says False, because 3 sits in the right subtree of 5 and is smaller than 5.

Why the swapped pair shows up as descents: a sorted sequence has none. Swapping two far-apart values creates two descents (take the bigger value of the first and the smaller value of the last); swapping neighbours creates one.

The contest shortcut. In Python there is no built-in balanced BST. When the keys arrive offline, a sorted list with bisect does the same job: insort keeps it sorted and the two functions below give floor and ceiling.

Exam traps

Duplicates: decide from the statement whether equal keys go left, right or are forbidden, and use the matching strict or non-strict bound. A BST built from sorted input is a linked list of height n: recursion that deep fails in Python, so walk iteratively. Seed the bounds with float('-inf') and float('inf'), not with a guess like 0 or 10⁹.

Remember

Validate with bounds from every ancestor, never with the parent alone.

BST inorder = sorted order; most BST questions are sorted-array questions in disguise.

Bridge to stop 5

Complete trees by numbers, and the priority queue idea

Big idea

A heap glues two separate ideas together: a promise (the priority queue: always hand out the most important item next) and a shape (the complete binary tree, which packs perfectly into an array with simple index arithmetic). Learn each one on its own and stop 5 is just the glue.

What versus how: abstract data types

An abstract data type (ADT) lists operations and what they promise, nothing about memory. A data structure is one way to keep those promises. A stack is an ADT (push, pop, last in first out); a Python list is one structure that implements it.

The priority queue ADT promises: insert(x), peek_max(), extract_max(). Several structures can keep that promise, at very different costs:

Implementationinsertpeek maxextract max
Unsorted listO(1) appendO(n) scanO(n) scan + remove
Sorted listO(n) shift to make roomO(1) last itemO(1) pop()
BST (stop 4)O(h)O(h) rightmostO(h): log n if balanced, n if skewed
Binary heap (stop 5)O(log n)O(1)O(log n), always

Each of the first three is fast at something and slow at something else. The heap is never the fastest at any single operation, but it is never slow, and its height is guaranteed to be log n because of its shape.

Numbering a complete tree level by level

A complete binary tree fills every level left to right with no gaps (only the last level may be partly full). Number its nodes in that reading order starting from 0, and the numbers fall into a pattern:

  • Level d starts at index 2ᵈ − 1 and holds 2ᵈ slots (1, 2, 4, 8, …).
  • Take node i, the j-th node on level d, so i = 2ᵈ − 1 + j. Its left child is the 2j-th node on level d + 1, at index 2ᵈ⁺¹ − 1 + 2j = 2(2ᵈ − 1 + j) + 1 = 2i + 1.
  • So the right child is 2i + 2, and going back up, the parent is (i − 1) // 2.

No pointers are needed: the array position is the tree position. This only works because there are no gaps, which is why a heap insists on being complete.

Fact about a complete tree with n nodesValuen = 12
Height (in edges)⌊log₂ n⌋3
Number of leaves⌈n / 2⌉6
First leaf (0-based)n // 26
Last node with a child (0-based)n // 2 − 15

That last row is where heap building starts in stop 5: leaves are already valid one-node heaps, so only indices n // 2 − 1 down to 0 need fixing.

Added: missing from your notes

0-based versus 1-based. CLRS numbers from 1: children 2i and 2i + 1, parent ⌊i/2⌋. Python lists start at 0: children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent (i − 1) // 2. Mixing the two is the classic heap bug. In an exam, say which convention you are using.

Remember
  • ADT = the promise; data structure = how it's kept. A heap implements a priority queue.
  • 0-based: children 2i + 1, 2i + 2; parent (i − 1) // 2.
  • n nodes: height ⌊log₂ n⌋, ⌈n/2⌉ leaves, last internal node n // 2 − 1.

Heaps and priority queues

Big idea

A structure built for one question: "who is the most important item right now?" Learn the two rules, the array trick, and the two moves (bubble up, sift down).

The problem a heap solves

A hospital emergency room needs three operations: add a patient, see who has the highest emergency score, and remove that patient. Let N be the number of waiting patients.

Designinsert(x)get_max()delete_max()Problem
Unsorted lineO(1)O(N)O(N)Must scan everyone to find the worst case
Sorted lineO(N)O(1)O(1)Insert must shift people to keep order
HeapO(log N)O(1)O(log N)Good at everything

The heap's trick is to keep just enough order: not fully sorted (expensive), only enough to know the maximum instantly.

Building the idea from scratch

  1. A sorted line is a path. What if we join many short sorted lines into a tree, so that every path from root down to a leaf is sorted?
  2. For every root-to-leaf path to be sorted (largest at top), each parent must be ≥ its children. This is the order property. Consequence: the maximum is at the root.
  3. For a fixed number of nodes, the shortest possible tree is one with every level full. That shape is a complete binary tree. Its height is about log₂N, so any root-to-leaf walk is short. This is the shape property.

The two rules

Remember

Max-heap = complete binary tree + every parent ≥ its children.
Min-heap = complete binary tree + every parent ≤ its children.

RuleMeaningWho maintains it
ShapeAll levels full except possibly the last; the last level is filled left to right with no gaps.Where we insert / which node we remove (always the last one).
OrderParent ≥ child (max-heap) at every node.Bubble up and sift down.
Exam trap

A heap is not a BST. In a heap, the left child is not required to be smaller than the right child. Siblings have no order. That is why searching for an arbitrary value in a heap is O(N), and why a heap cannot print sorted output by a simple inorder walk. A heap only promises: the top is the best.

Heap basics: the definition, rule by rule

Remember

Definition. A heap is a binary tree that satisfies two rules at once: a shape rule (it is a complete binary tree) and an order rule (every parent is ordered against its children). A max-heap requires parent ≥ child. A min-heap requires parent ≤ child.

Rule 1: the shape rule (complete binary tree)

Number the levels from the top: the root is level 0, its children level 1, and so on. A tree is complete when:

  1. Every level is completely full, except possibly the very last one.
  2. The last level is filled from left to right with no gaps.

Practical meaning: to add a node, you put it in the first free slot reading level by level, left to right. To remove a node, you remove the last one in that reading order. This is why heaps never get lopsided: their height is always about log₂ n.

Rule 2: the order rule

The order rule compares only a parent with its own children:

  • Max-heap: value(parent) ≥ value(each child). Consequently the largest value is at the root.
  • Min-heap: value(parent) ≤ value(each child). Consequently the smallest value is at the root.

Equal values are allowed (that is why we write ≥ and ≤). Crucially, siblings are not compared with each other, and a node is not compared with its cousins or with nodes in other branches.

Setup: storing a heap in an array

Because of the shape rule, the heap occupies positions 0, 1, 2, …, n−1 of an array with no gaps. The array is just the tree read level by level, left to right. To read an array as a heap: write the first element as the root, the next two as its children, the next four as the next level, and so on.

Array0123456
Values50304010203525
Level012

Check each parent against its children using the index formulas (children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2): index 0 (50) vs 30, 40 ✓; index 1 (30) vs 10, 20 ✓; index 2 (40) vs 35, 25 ✓. All parents are ≥ children, so this array is a valid max-heap. The checker lab below does this test for any array and shows you exactly which parent-child pairs break the rule.

A heap is the best compromise when you only ever care about the top item.

Storing a heap in an array (no pointers!)

Because the shape is always "complete", the tree can be stored level by level, left to right, in a plain array. Parent and children are found by arithmetic.

Relationship0-indexed (your notes)1-indexed (CLRS)
Left child of i2i + 12i
Right child of i2i + 22i + 1
Parent of i⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋⌊i / 2⌋
First leaf⌊n / 2⌋⌊n / 2⌋ + 1

Insert: bubble up (O(log n))

  1. Put the new value at the next free slot (end of the array). This keeps the shape rule.
  2. The order rule may now be broken between the new node and its parent. While the new node is bigger than its parent, swap them (move up one level).
  3. Stop when the parent is ≥ the node or you reach the root.

The node climbs at most one level per swap and there are about log₂n levels, so the cost is O(log n).

Worked example

Insert 9 into [15, 8, 10, 6, 3, 5, 7, 2, 1]. New slot is index 9, parent index 4 (value 3).

StepArrayReason
place15 8 10 6 3 5 7 2 1 9index 9
compare 9 with parent 3 (index 4)15 8 10 6 9 5 7 2 1 39 > 3, swap
compare 9 with parent 8 (index 1)15 9 10 6 8 5 7 2 1 39 > 8, swap
compare 9 with parent 15 (index 0)15 9 10 6 8 5 7 2 1 315 ≥ 9, stop. Two swaps.

Delete max: sift down (O(log n))

The max is the root, so removing it leaves a hole at the top and breaks both rules. The repair is neat:

  1. Swap the root with the last node, then remove the last slot. Shape is fixed instantly (we removed the last position). The old max is gone.
  2. The new root is probably small and breaks the order. Sift down: compare it with its two children, swap it with the larger child, and repeat from there.
  3. Stop when it is ≥ both children, or it has none.
Exam trap

Swap with the larger child, not just any child. If you swap with the smaller child, that smaller child becomes the parent of the larger sibling and the order rule is broken again.

Worked example

Delete the max (15) from [15, 8, 10, 6, 3, 5, 7, 2, 1].

StepArrayReason
swap root with last, drop last1 8 10 6 3 5 7 21 is now at the root; 15 returned
children of root: 8, 1010 8 1 6 3 5 7 210 is larger: swap with 10
children of index 2: 5, 710 8 7 6 3 5 1 27 is larger: swap with 7
index 6 has no children10 8 7 6 3 5 1 2Stop. Valid heap.

Build a heap from N items: O(N), not O(N log N)

Inserting N items one at a time costs O(N log N). There is a faster way: dump the array in as is, then fix it from the bottom up. Leaves are already valid one-node heaps, so start at the last non-leaf (index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1) and sift down each node, moving toward index 0.

Worked example

Build from [4, 10, 3, 5, 1]. n = 5, start at i = 1. Node 10 (children 5 and 1): already ≥ both, fine. Then i = 0: node 4 has children 10 and 3, swap with 10 → [10, 4, 3, 5, 1]; 4 now at index 1 with children 5 and 1, swap with 5 → [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]. Done: a valid max-heap in 2 swaps.

Added: missing from your notes

Why O(N)? (CLRS 6.3) Sifting a node costs O(its height), not O(log n). Half the nodes are leaves (height 0, free). A quarter have height 1, an eighth height 2, and so on. In general at most ⌈n/2h+1⌉ nodes have height h. Total = Σ over h of (n / 2h+1) · O(h) = O(n · Σ h/2h) = O(n), because the sum Σ h/2h converges to 2. Most nodes are near the bottom and travel only a short distance.

Heap sort

Build a max-heap in O(n). Then repeat: swap the root (largest) with the last unsorted position, shrink the heap by one, and sift down the new root. After n−1 rounds the array is sorted ascending. Time O(n log n) in all cases, space O(1), not stable.

heap sortO(n log n)In place
Added: missing from your notes

Priority queue is the abstract idea (insert, get best, remove best). A heap is the standard way to implement it. CLRS names: HEAP-MAXIMUM, HEAP-EXTRACT-MAX, HEAP-INCREASE-KEY, MAX-HEAP-INSERT. In Python, heapq is a min-heap on a list; for a max-heap, push negated values.

Problem solving using heaps

Spot the pattern: "repeatedly take the smallest/largest", "top k", "merge sorted streams", "median of a stream".

1. The k-th largest element

Counter-intuitive: use a min-heap of size k. It always holds the k largest seen so far, and its top (the smallest of those k) is the k-th largest. Any new value smaller than the top cannot be among the k largest.

Worked example

nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2. Heap after each item: [3] → [2,3] → 1 is smaller than 2, ignore → 5 > 2, heap [3,5] → 6 > 3, heap [5,6] → 4 < 5, ignore. Top = 5, the 2nd largest. The heap holds the two largest: 5 and 6.

2. Running median (two heaps)

Keep the lower half of the numbers in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, with sizes differing by at most 1. The median is at the top of one heap (or the average of both tops). Each insertion is O(log n), reading the median is O(1).

3. Merge k sorted lists

Put the first element of each list in a min-heap (with its list id). Pop the smallest, output it, push the next element from the same list. N total elements, heap size k → O(N log k).

4. Connect ropes at minimum cost

Cost of joining two ropes is the sum of their lengths. Greedy: always join the two shortest. Min-heap: pop two, push their sum, add the sum to the cost. O(n log n).

5. Other classics

  • Top k frequent elements: count with a dictionary, keep a size-k min-heap on counts.
  • Sort a nearly-sorted array (each element at most k places off): a min-heap of size k+1 gives O(n log k).
  • Task scheduling / CPU scheduling / Dijkstra's shortest path: all use a priority queue as the engine.
Teacher's note

Whenever a brute force keeps doing "scan everything to find the biggest/smallest", ask: can a heap hand me that in O(log n) instead of O(n)? That one question solves most heap problems.

Patterns for contests: heaps

Seen in your contests

Contest 1: Q2 second minimum of a min-heap (it is the smaller of the root’s two children, min(heap[1], heap[2]), never a scan of everything) and Q3 insertion in O(log n) with heapq forbidden: bubble up by hand (20/40). Mid-sem Q3 was array to min-heap, which is the O(n) build from this stop.

PatternWords in the statementTool
Implement the heap“without heapq”, “O(log n) per insertion”array, parent (i − 1) // 2, bubble up and sift down
k-way merge“k sorted lists”, “k-th smallest pair sum”heap of (value, list, position)

Rooms and machines“fewest rooms”, “earliest free”min-heap of end times

Exam traps

heapq is a min-heap only: store negatives for a max-heap. Tuples compare left to right, so put the priority first and add an index as a tie-breaker if the second item can’t be compared. “Touching” meetings (end = next start) share a room when the check is <=. Sifting down: compare with both children and swap with the smaller one.

Remember

Heap = the best item now, in O(log n). Sort by when things become available, then pop the best.

No heapq allowed: array + bubble up + sift down, both O(log n).
