connect everything as cheaply as possibleMST: Kruskal or PrimO(E log V)

Not sure which row you are in? Section 8 is a decision page with the questions in the order to ask them.

1. Order without cycles: topological sort

If a graph has no directed cycle (a DAG), its vertices can be listed so that every edge goes from earlier to later. “Course b before course a”, “build step 1 before step 2”, and “this cell leads to a bigger cell” are all DAGs. There are two standard ways to get the order, and both detect a cycle for free.

Kahn’s algorithm (peeling). A vertex that nothing points to can safely go first. Remove it, lower the in-degree of everything it points to, repeat. If some vertices never reach in-degree 0, they lie on or behind a cycle.

Hand trace on the graph 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1 (queue shown after each pop; ties by index):

PopIn-degrees of 0 1 2 3 4 5 afterwardsQueueOrder so far
start2 2 1 1 0 04, 5
41 1 1 1 0 054
50 1 0 1 0 02, 04 5
20 1 0 0 0 00, 34 5 2
00 1 0 0 0 034 5 2 0
30 0 0 0 0 014 5 2 0 3
10 0 0 0 0 04 5 2 0 3 1

DFS version. Run DFS and list vertices in reverse finishing order: a vertex finishes only after everything it points to has finished, so it ends up before them in the reversed list. Three colours (unseen, on the current path, finished) detect cycles: meeting a vertex that is on the current path means a back edge, which means a cycle. This version is iterative, so a 200,000-long chain cannot hit Python’s recursion limit.

Course Schedule. LC 207 only asks whether an order exists; LC 210 asks for one. Note the direction: [a, b] means b comes before a, so the edge is b → a.

DP over a DAG

In a DAG the topological order is a valid order to fill a DP table: by the time you reach u, every path into u has already been accounted for. So shortest and longest paths, even with negative weights, need no heap: process vertices in topological order and relax their out-edges once. Longest path is NP-hard on general graphs but easy here, because there are no cycles to loop around. Counting paths is the same loop with + in place of min.

Contest problems that are secretly DAGs

LC 329 Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix. Draw an edge from each cell to every bigger neighbour: a DAG, because values strictly increase. The longest path is the number of Kahn layers. The usual memoised DFS recurses up to 40,000 levels on a 200×200 grid, which exceeds Python’s default recursion limit of 1,000; peeling avoids recursion entirely.

LC 1857 Largest Color Value in a Directed Graph. Keep, for every vertex, the best count of each of the 26 colours on any path ending there, and push it forward in topological order. If Kahn does not reach every vertex there is a cycle and the answer is −1. A self-loop never reaches in-degree 0, so it is caught the same way.

Practice

LC 207, LC 210, LC 802 (peel the reversed graph), LC 329, LC 1857, CSES Course Schedule, CSES Longest Flight Route. All the code above was checked against brute force on random graphs, including cyclic ones.

2. Dijkstra: BFS with a heap

BFS finds the fewest edges. With weights a longer route can be lighter: in the lab graph, 0 → 1 directly costs 4, but 0 → 2 → 1 costs 1 + 2 = 3. Dijkstra’s rule: always finish the closest unfinished vertex next. Python’s heapq is a min-heap of tuples, so a heap of (distance, vertex) pops the closest first.

Hand trace on 0→1 (4), 0→2 (1), 2→1 (2), 1→3 (1), 2→3 (5), 3→4 (3). Entries are (distance, vertex); notice the two stale pops, which the d > dist[u] check skips:

Popdist for 0 1 2 3 4 afterwardsHeap contents
(0, 0)0 4 1 ∞ ∞(1,2) (4,1)
(1, 2)0 3 1 6 ∞(3,1) (4,1) (6,3)
(3, 1)0 3 1 4 ∞(4,1) (4,3) (6,3)
(4, 1)stale: dist[1] is already 3, skip
(4, 3)0 3 1 4 7(6,3) (7,4)
(6, 3)stale, skip
(7, 4)0 3 1 4 7empty

The “from” array ends as −, 2, 0, 1, 3, so the path to vertex 4 is 0 → 2 → 1 → 3 → 4 with cost 7.

Cost. Each vertex is expanded once and each edge pushes at most one entry, so there are at most E pushes and pops, each O(log E) = O(log V): O((V + E) log V). For an undirected graph add each edge in both directions.

Why it is correct, and why negative edges break it

Claim: when (d, u) is popped and is not stale, d is the true shortest distance to u. Any other route to u must leave the set of finished vertices through some edge into an unfinished vertex x. That x is still in the heap with a value of at least d (u was the smallest), and the rest of the route can only add non-negative weight, so it cannot come in below d. The proof uses exactly one assumption: extending a path never makes it cheaper.

A negative edge breaks that assumption. On 0→1 (2), 0→2 (3), 2→1 (−2) the textbook version below finalises vertex 1 at distance 2 and never looks again, although 0 → 2 → 1 costs 1. It returns 2, which is wrong:

The stale-check template above would, on this tiny graph, expand vertex 1 a second time and recover the answer 1. Do not rely on that: re-expanding vertices voids the O((V + E) log V) bound (on adversarial graphs it can take exponential time), and a negative cycle makes it loop forever. With negative edges use Bellman–Ford.

Dijkstra on grids, and “minimise the maximum”

A grid is a graph whose vertices are cells and whose edges join neighbours (stop 6.5). Dijkstra works whenever the cost of a path is built so that extending it never lowers it, and that includes more than sums. In LC 1631 Path With Minimum Effort the cost of a path is its largest height difference, so replace d + w by max(d, w). LC 778 Swim in Rising Water is the same with the cell height as the cost. LC 1514 Path With Maximum Probability maximises a product of numbers at most 1: store negated probabilities in the min-heap.

For “minimise the maximum” there is a second solution that is often shorter to write: binary search the answer, with a plain BFS answering “can I get there if no step may exceed x?”. It costs O(cells · log(range)).

Practice

LC 743, LC 1631 (both ways), LC 1514, LC 778, LC 1976, CSES Shortest Routes I. The grid and probability versions were checked against an exhaustive relaxation on random inputs.

3. When the weights are 0 or 1

A free edge keeps you on the same level, so its end goes to the front of the deque; a cost-1 edge goes to the back. The deque always holds at most two distance values, in order, so no heap is needed: O(V + E).

4. An extra rule: free passes

“Up to k edges on your path cost nothing” is the node-is-a-state idea with weights: the node is (vertex, passes used), and each edge can be taken normally or with a pass.

5. Negative edges: Bellman–Ford, and all pairs: Floyd–Warshall

Why V − 1 rounds are enough. If there is no negative cycle, some shortest path to every vertex is simple (a repeated vertex would mean a cycle of weight ≥ 0 that can be cut out), so it has at most V − 1 edges. One round relaxes every edge once. After round r, the distance of every vertex is at most the cost of its best path with at most r edges, because the last edge of such a path is relaxed in round r. So after V − 1 rounds all distances are final. Negative cycle: run one more round; if anything still improves, a reachable negative cycle exists and shortest distances are undefined.

Hand trace on the textbook graph (CLRS), source 0, edges relaxed in the order 0→1 (6), 0→2 (7), 1→2 (8), 1→3 (5), 1→4 (−4), 2→3 (−3), 2→4 (9), 3→1 (−2), 4→3 (7), 4→0 (2). Because the code updates dist in place, later edges in a round can already use values improved earlier in the same round, so it may settle in fewer rounds than the worst case:

Afterdist for 0 1 2 3 4
start0 ∞ ∞ ∞ ∞
round 10 2 7 4 2
round 20 2 7 4 −2
rounds 3 and 4no change; the extra check pass finds no improvement, so no negative cycle

“At most k edges”: LC 787

“At most k stops” means at most k + 1 edges, so run exactly k + 1 rounds. Here the in-place shortcut is a bug: it could let a round use two edges. Read from the old row and write to a copy, so each round adds exactly one edge:

Floyd–Warshall: all pairs

Let dk[i][j] be the shortest i → j distance using only vertices 0..k−1 as intermediate stops. Either the best route avoids k, or it goes i → k → j: dk+1[i][j] = min(dk[i][j], dk[i][k] + dk[k][j]). The k loop must be outermost because the table must be complete for k − 1 before k is allowed. Time O(V³), space O(V²), so only for V up to a few hundred. LC 1334 is the standard use: count the cities within the threshold from every city.

Practice

LC 787, LC 1334, LC 2290 and LC 1368 (0-1 BFS), CSES Shortest Routes II, CSES High Score (positive cycle). Both functions were checked against exhaustive path enumeration.

6. Minimum spanning trees

A spanning tree of a connected graph uses V − 1 edges and connects every vertex with no cycle. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is one of least total weight. Think of laying cable to connect every town for the lowest cost.

Two facts justify every MST algorithm:

  • Cut property. Split the vertices into two non-empty groups. A lightest edge crossing between the groups belongs to some MST (to every MST if it is the unique lightest crossing edge).
  • Cycle property. On any cycle, an edge that is strictly heavier than all the others on that cycle belongs to no MST.

Why the cut property holds: take any MST without that edge e. Adding e creates a cycle, which must cross the cut a second time through some edge f. Swapping f for e keeps a spanning tree and its weight does not go up, because e was a lightest crossing edge.

Kruskal: sort the edges, keep the ones that join two pieces

Process edges from lightest to heaviest. An edge is kept if its endpoints are in different components (union-find answers this), and skipped if it would close a cycle. When Kruskal keeps edge e joining components A and B, e is the lightest edge leaving A (anything lighter was processed earlier and either joined things or lay inside a component), so the cut property says keeping it is safe. The union-find below uses path halving and union by size, which together make each operation almost constant (inverse Ackermann; see the appendix stop). Cost: sorting dominates, O(E log E) = O(E log V).

Hand trace: edges 0–1 (4), 0–2 (3), 1–2 (1), 1–3 (2), 2–3 (4), 3–4 (2), 4–5 (6), 3–5 (7); vertices 0..5.

Edge (sorted)DecisionTotal
1–2 (1)keep1
1–3 (2)keep3
3–4 (2)keep5
0–2 (3)keep8
0–1 (4)skip: 0 and 1 already connected8
2–3 (4)skip: cycle8
4–5 (6)keep14
3–5 (7)skip: cycle14

Five edges kept = V − 1, total 14. If fewer than V − 1 edges are kept, the graph is disconnected and there is no spanning tree.

Prim: grow one tree, always take the cheapest edge leaving it

Start anywhere. Repeatedly add the lightest edge from the tree to a vertex outside it; the tree versus the rest is a cut, so the cut property applies every time. It is Dijkstra with one change: the heap key is the single edge entering the tree, not the distance from the source. Entries for vertices already in the tree are stale and skipped, as in Dijkstra.

KruskalPrim (heap)Prim (no heap, adjacency matrix)
TimeO(E log V)O(E log V)O(V²)
Needsedge list, union-findadjacency list, heapdistance array only
Prefer whengraph is sparse; edges arrive as a list; you also want to know which edges merge componentsgraph is sparse and you already have adjacency listsgraph is dense or complete, such as points in a plane (V² ≈ E)

Both give a tree of the same total weight (the tree itself can differ when weights tie). With all distinct weights the MST is unique. Checked on random graphs against every spanning tree.

MST problems in contests

LC 1584 Min Cost to Connect All Points is a complete graph with Manhattan distances, so use heap-free Prim, O(n²). LC 684 Redundant Connection: add edges in input order; the first one whose endpoints are already connected closes the cycle. LC 1135 Connecting Cities is plain Kruskal with a −1 answer if fewer than V − 1 edges are kept.

LC 1489 Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges (harder). An edge is critical if every MST uses it: banning it makes the best tree heavier or impossible. It is pseudo-critical if some MST uses it but not all: forcing it in still gives the optimal weight. With n ≤ 100 and m ≤ 200, running Kruskal about 2m times is fast enough.

Practice

LC 1584, LC 684, LC 1135, LC 1489, CSES Road Reparation, LC 1202 and LC 721 (union-find). A useful side fact: the path between two vertices in an MST also minimises the largest edge on any route between them, which is why “minimise the maximum” problems (section 2) can also be solved with Kruskal.

7. Union-find, and running time backwards

Reverse-time trick (CF 722C). DSU can merge but not split. When a problem removes things one by one and asks for something after each removal, run time backwards: start empty and add them in reverse order.

8. Choosing the right graph algorithm

Ask these in order and stop at the first yes.

#Question about the problemUse
1Is there an order or dependency (“before”, “prerequisite”, “builds on”)?Topological sort (Kahn); DP in that order if you need a best value. A cycle means no answer.
2Do you need to connect everything at least total cost, rather than reach one target?MST: Kruskal, or heap-free Prim if the graph is dense.
3Do you only ask “are these connected?” as edges arrive, or merge groups?Union-find.
4Is the cost the largest edge on the path, or a “minimise the maximum”?Dijkstra with max, binary search plus BFS, or Kruskal.
5All edges cost the same (or you count edges)?BFS (multi-source if there are several starts).
6All weights are 0 or 1?0-1 BFS.
7Are some weights negative?DAG: topological DP. Otherwise Bellman–Ford (and it spots negative cycles).
8“At most k edges / stops”?Bellman–Ford for exactly k rounds, or Dijkstra on (node, steps used).
9An extra rule (passes, parity, keys, time)?Make the state (node, extra), then BFS or Dijkstra on states.
10Shortest paths between all pairs and V ≤ about 400?Floyd–Warshall.
11Weights are non-negative and you want from one source?Dijkstra.

The constraints help too: V ≤ 400 allows O(V³); V, E ≤ 10⁵ needs O(E log V) or better; V ≤ 20 points to a bitmask over the vertices.

9. Try these by hand

Do each on paper before opening the answer. They are the dry-run shapes the written part of an exam and the mock interview ask for.

  1. Kahn. Edges 0→2, 1→2, 2→3, 1→3, 3→4 on vertices 0..4. Write the in-degrees, then the queue and order after each pop.
    AnswerIn-degrees 0 0 2 2 1. Queue 0, 1; pop 0 (vertex 2 drops to 1); pop 1 (vertex 2 reaches 0 and joins the queue, vertex 3 drops to 1); pop 2 (vertex 3 reaches 0); pop 3; pop 4. Order 0 1 2 3 4.
  2. Dijkstra table. Edges 0→1 (2), 0→2 (5), 1→2 (1), 1→3 (7), 2→3 (2), source 0. List every heap pop.
    AnswerPops: (0,0), (2,1), (3,2), (5,2) stale, (5,3), (9,3) stale. Final distances 0 2 3 5; the predecessor of 3 is 2.
  3. Bellman–Ford. Edges in this order: 2→3 (−2), 1→2 (3), 0→1 (4), 0→3 (9); source 0, four vertices. Show dist after each round.
    AnswerRound 1: 0 4 ∞ 9. Round 2: 0 4 7 9. Round 3: 0 4 7 5 (the edge 2→3 finally fires). The check pass finds no improvement. This order is deliberately the worst case: it needs all V − 1 = 3 rounds.
  4. Kruskal. Edges 0–1 (5), 1–2 (3), 0–2 (4), 2–3 (1), 1–3 (6). Which are kept, and what is the total?
    AnswerSorted: 2–3 keep, 1–2 keep, 0–2 keep, 0–1 skip (cycle), 1–3 skip (cycle). Total 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.
Exam traps

In BFS you mark a vertex when you push it; in Dijkstra a vertex is final only when popped, because a cheaper route can still arrive (see the spot-the-bug drill). Dijkstra needs “extending a path never makes it cheaper”: negative edges violate it. Undirected graphs need both directions in the adjacency list. Kahn returning fewer than n vertices means a cycle, not a bug. Course prerequisites [a, b] point b → a. A recursive DFS on 10⁵ levels will crash in Python. Floyd–Warshall needs the k loop outermost. For “at most k edges” read the old row. Prim and Kruskal can return different trees of equal weight when weights tie.

Remember

Kahn: queue every in-degree-0 vertex, peel, repeat. Fewer than n out → cycle. DFS: reverse finishing order; an edge into a vertex on the current path → cycle.

Dijkstra: pop smallest, skip stale, relax; final on pop. No negative edges. “Max of the path” → max(d, w).

Weights 0/1 → deque. Negative → Bellman–Ford (V − 1 rounds, one more to detect a cycle). At most k edges → k + 1 rounds on a copy. Extra rule → states. All pairs, small V → Floyd, k outermost.

MST: cut property (lightest crossing edge is safe), cycle property (heaviest on a cycle is out). Kruskal: sort edges, keep what union() accepts, V − 1 kept or disconnected. Prim: grow a tree with a heap, or O(V²) on dense graphs.

Removals asked? Run time backwards. Practice: the Ladder, tab Graphs II.

Sorting and trees line · a stop your outline lists

Monotonic stacks and queues

Big idea

A monotonic stack keeps its contents in sorted order by popping everything that can no longer matter before pushing the new item. That one rule turns “for each element, find the nearest bigger/smaller one” from O(n²) into O(n): every element is pushed once and popped once. Your course outline lists monotonic stacks as a feature; this stop is where they live. The monotonic deque is the same idea with the front also expiring, for sliding windows.

Words in the statementTool
“next greater”, “next warmer day”, “previous smaller”, “stock span”stack of indices; pop while the top is beaten
“largest rectangle”, “widest range where this is the minimum”the popped element’s left and right boundaries
“sum over all subarrays of the minimum (or maximum)”count each element’s contribution: left span × right span
“smallest number / lexicographically smallest after removing k”pop while the top is bigger than the new item and removals remain
“maximum of every window of size k”monotonic deque
“trapped water”two pointers, or a stack of walls
“pairs that can see each other”stack of (height, count)

The template: next greater element

The stack holds indices whose answer is still unknown, with decreasing values. A new value that beats the top is the answer for everything it beats.

Dry run on [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]: push 0; 1 doesn’t beat 2, push 1; the second 2 beats index 1 (answer 2), not index 0 (equal), push 2; 4 beats indices 2 and 0 (answer 3), push 3; 3 beats nothing, push 4. Result [3, 2, 3, −1, −1]. Strict versus non-strict comparison (< versus <=) is the one decision that changes with the wording “greater” or “greater or equal”.

Histogram: each bar, as the shortest bar of a rectangle

Contribution counting, and the tie-break that avoids double counting

Sum of the minimum over all subarrays: element i is the minimum of (distance to the previous smaller) × (distance to the next smaller) subarrays. With equal values both sides would count the same subarray, so make one side strict and the other non-strict.

Remove k digits, sliding window, rain water

A pairs problem: Visible Pairs

Count pairs of people who can see each other when nobody between them is taller than the shorter of the two. The stack holds (height, how many people have it) so that equal heights, which really happen, are counted once per person. It’s in the Vault on the Ladder with the full statement; the solution is:

Every function on this page was checked against an O(n²) or O(n³) brute force on random inputs.

Exam traps

Store indices, not values, when you need distances. Decide strict versus non-strict from the statement’s wording about equal values. Flush the stack at the end (a sentinel 0 in the histogram) or the last bars never get an answer. Pop in a while, not an if. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so the whole thing is O(n) even though there’s a loop inside a loop.

Remember

Pop what can’t matter any more, then push. Next/previous greater/smaller in O(n).

Min or max over all subarrays: each element’s contribution = left span × right span, one side strict.

Sliding window maximum: a deque whose front expires.

Practice: the Ladder, tab Monotonic stack.

Foundations line · Python, limits, routine, tricks

Contest toolkit

Big idea

Contests reward the same small set of habits: read the limits first, write a brute force, trust nothing you haven’t stress-tested, and know your standard library so no minute is lost to typing. This stop collects them, plus the Python tools and tricks that sit just outside the lecture notes but pay off on every topic.

Ratings: Codeforces and LeetCode, side by side

The Ladder shows both. CF ratings come from Codeforces contests (a problem rated 1600 is solved by about half of the contestants rated 1600). LC ratings are the community estimates for LeetCode contest problems; classics that never appeared in a contest have none. The two scales aren’t officially linked and LeetCode’s run higher. This notebook uses a rough rule, LC rating − 400 ≈ CF rating, and marks every converted number with ≈. Your teacher’s hardest end-sem rung is a typical Div. 2 C (CF 1600): an easy pattern behind one real observation.

Constraints tell you the algorithm

ConstraintAim forUsually means
n ≤ 10O(n!)try every ordering
n ≤ 20O(2ⁿ)every subset, backtracking, bitmask
n ≤ 40O(2^(n/2))meet in the middle
n ≤ 500O(n³)Floyd–Warshall, DP over triples
n ≤ 5,000O(n²)DP over pairs, a walk from every node
n ≤ 2·10⁵O(n log n)sort, heap, binary search, BFS/DFS, monotonic stack
n ≤ 10¹⁸O(log n)binary lifting, fast power, a formula

Python manages about 10⁷ simple operations per second, so the useful budget is smaller than in C++: an O(n²) with n = 5,000 (2.5·10⁷) is borderline, and 10⁵ squared is hopeless.

The routine for every problem

  1. Read the constraints and the subtasks before the story. Write down what each limit allows.
  2. Work one example by hand and restate the problem in one line using graph, DP or sorting words.
  3. Write the most obvious correct solution (simulate, try everything). Aim for about 10 minutes.
  4. Submit it. Marks are in the bank before you start thinking hard.
  5. Use it as a microscope: print its answers for tiny inputs and look for what repeats or stays fixed.
  6. Write the fast version, stress-test it against the brute force, then submit.

On the unseen hard problems of the end-sem, steps 3 and 4 are worth more than any single clever idea: Chakravyuh’s first subtask needed only an eight-line brute force.

TopicEdge cases to try in your head
Graphn = 1; no edges; several components; unreachable target (return −1?); start equals target; self-loops, repeated edges
Gridone row or column; everything blocked; start blocked; the answer is 0
DPsmallest n (0, 1, 2); all values equal; impossible states (−1 or ∞, never 0); modulo after every addition
Greedyties in the sort key; touching intervals; negative values; an empty selection
Arrayslength 1; all equal; already sorted; sorted backwards; maximum values (overflow is not a Python problem, speed is)

Stress testing: let the brute force check you

Run both versions on thousands of tiny random inputs and stop at the first disagreement. Tiny inputs matter: the failing case is small enough to trace by hand. This one catches the “at most two coins” trap from Contest 2 Q1 when values can be negative:

It prints a mismatch such as MISMATCH on [-1] brute 0 fast -1 (the exact case varies): with only a negative coin, taking none beats taking one. The fix is to ignore negative values, sum(x for x in sorted(c)[-2:] if x > 0); rerun, and silence means you can submit.

Python for contests

Input and output. Calling input() hundreds of thousands of times is slow on its own; read everything once and print once. Unseen Codeforces problems use standard input and usually several test cases:

“The sum of n over all test cases is at most 2·10⁵” means you size arrays per test, never at the maximum for every test.

The standard library you should have in your fingers.

ToolUse it for
bisect_left / bisect_right / insortbinary search on a sorted list; floor, ceiling, count of values below x; LIS
heapq (heappush, heappop, heapreplace, nsmallest, merge)priority queues, Dijkstra, k-way merge, top-k

collections.Counterfrequencies, “most common”, comparing multisets

Speed. Local variables are faster than globals, so put the work inside a function. List comprehensions beat explicit loops. Lists of lists beat defaultdict(list) when keys are 0 to n − 1. Appending to a string with += in a loop is fine in CPython, but join a list when in doubt. Some judges run PyPy, which is much faster on plain loops but slower at some built-ins: use whichever interpreter the judge uses and test with it.

Hash-map attacks. On Codeforces some tests are built to make Python’s dict and set collide and slow to a crawl. If a hash-heavy solution times out for no visible reason, sort instead (bisect on a sorted list) or XOR the keys with a random 32-bit number before inserting.

Deep recursion. The default limit is about 1,000 calls. Prefer an explicit stack or queue for graphs and write DP bottom-up. When you must recurse deeply, raise the limit and run in a thread with a big stack:

Floats. Compare with a tolerance, or avoid floats: ratios as fractions of integers, square roots with isqrt.

Array tricks that appear everywhere

Binary search on the answer. “Minimise the maximum”, “smallest x such that …”: if “can it be done with value x?” goes False, False, …, True, True as x grows, search for the first True. You only write the yes/no check, often a greedy or a BFS.

Prefix sums, difference arrays and a sliding window. Prefix sums turn “sum of a range” into a subtraction, and with a dictionary they count subarrays with a given sum even with negatives. A difference array applies many range additions in O(n + ops). A window whose left end never moves back finds the shortest subarray with a large enough sum in O(n).

Fenwick tree. Prefix sums with point updates in O(log n): the first step beyond the course when a problem mixes “change one value” with “sum of a range”.

Dynamic programming and greedy line · tree DP, DAG DP, binary search, union-find, heaps, trie

Bridges: tools you know, combined

Big idea

You already know trees, heaps, DP, graphs and union-find. Contest problems rarely use one tool alone. This stop shows six combinations that appear again and again: DP on a tree, DP on a DAG, binary search plus a check, union-find for more than MST, heaps with greedy, and the trie. None is a new idea; each is two familiar ideas snapped together. It goes slightly beyond the written outline, and every function below was tested.

1. DP on a tree

A tree’s subproblems are its subtrees, and the order is “children before parent”. Compute a small answer for every node from its children’s answers. The simplest safe way to get that order is a stack that lists nodes parent-first, then reversed: every child then comes before its parent, with no recursion, so a 10⁵-long chain cannot crash Python.

  • LC 337 House Robber III. Two numbers per node: best if you rob it, best if you skip it.
  • LC 543 Diameter. A path bends at one node; its length is the left height plus the right height.
  • LC 124 Maximum Path Sum. Going up a path may use only one branch; a path that bends here may use both. Ignore negative branches.

2. DP on a DAG

Any DAG (see stop 12) is a “tree with sharing”: fill the table in topological order. Shortest path, longest path, number of paths, and LC 329 and LC 1857 are all this. The recipe never changes: define the value at a vertex from its predecessors, process vertices in topological order, and a cycle means no answer.

3. Binary search on the answer, with a graph check

If “can we do it with limit x?” is easy to check, and the answer to that question changes from no to yes exactly once as x grows, binary search x. Typical checks are a BFS (LC 1631, 778), a greedy scan (LC 875 Koko, LC 1011 ship packages, LC 410 split array) or a union-find over the edges at most x. The check in LC 1631 appears in stop 12 beside the Dijkstra version; solving a problem two ways and comparing is the best way to catch a mistake. The generic pattern is first_true in stop 14.

4. Union-find beyond MST

Union-find also answers “which items end up in one group?” LC 721 Accounts Merge: two accounts sharing an email are the same person, so union all emails of an account. LC 399 Evaluate Division: a weighted union-find stores each node’s ratio to its parent, so a query is a ratio of two ratios to the same root. Both use an iterative find, so long chains are safe. LC 2092 (union by time) and CF 722C (run time backwards) are on the Ladder.

5. Heaps with greedy

Stop 5 has the one-heap patterns: top-k, k-way merge, meeting rooms and “best available now”. A new one is two heaps meeting at the middle, for a running median (LC 295): a max-heap holds the smaller half, a min-heap the larger half, and their tops are the median.

6. The trie

A trie is a tree with one child per letter; a word is a path ending in a marker. Insert, search and prefix queries cost O(length of the word), independent of how many words are stored. It pairs with backtracking: LC 212 Word Search II walks the grid and the trie together, so a path that matches no prefix is cut at once, and a branch whose words are all found is deleted.

Exam traps

Tree DP with recursion fails on deep trees in Python. In the running median, rebalance after every insert. A trie’s starts_with on an empty prefix is always true; LeetCode prefixes are never empty. The check function in a binary search must be monotone, or the search returns nonsense. A weighted union-find must compress paths and fix the ratios while doing it.

Remember

Tree DP: children first (reverse of parent-first), two numbers per node when a choice depends on the parent. DAG DP: topological order. Binary search: “is x enough?” must flip once. DSU: merge things that must be together; weighted DSU stores ratios or parities. Two heaps: smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap. Trie: path = word.

Contest readiness

Big idea

By now you know the algorithms. Contest marks are lost to things around the algorithm: choosing the wrong one, a Python slip, an edge case, or running out of clock. This stop is the final checklist: constraints that tell you the algorithm, the Python pitfalls that cost marks, one sheet of templates to type from memory, how to explain a solution out loud for the Mock AI Interview, and a full three-hour mock contest with answers.

1. Constraints tell you the algorithm

2. Python pitfalls that cost marks

The function below demonstrates five of them with the values you will see (shown in the comments). The rest are in the list underneath.

  • Recursion limit. Python allows about 1,000 nested calls. DFS on a long chain, a skewed tree, or a deep memoised DP crashes. Write the iterative version (stacks, topological peeling) or convert to a table. Raising the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit may still overflow the real stack.
  • Slow input. For 10⁵ numbers use sys.stdin.readline or read everything once (template in stop 14).
  • Costly operations. list.pop(0) and x in list are O(n): use deque and set. s += c in a loop and slices like a[i:] copy; use indices.
  • heapq. A min-heap only (negate for max); tuples compare element by element, so a tie on the first value compares the second and may fail on objects that cannot be compared; there is no decrease-key, so push a new entry and skip stale ones.
  • Integer division and modulo round toward −∞, not toward zero.
  • Floats. Compare with a tolerance, or work in integers.

4. Explain it out loud (Mock AI Interview, 10%)

The interview asks conceptual questions and hands-on coding. For every algorithm you can code, be able to say four things in under a minute: what it does, the invariant (what stays true each step), the complexity and why, and the edge cases you would test. Then dry-run it on a three-element input.

AlgorithmInvariant to stateCost to justify
Quick Sort partitioneverything left of the scan pointer is ≤ pivotO(n log n) average, O(n²) worst if splits are lopsided
Heap sift downboth subtrees are heapsO(log n): one path of the tree
BFSvertices leave the queue in order of distanceO(V + E): each vertex and edge once
Kahnthe queue holds exactly the vertices with no unfinished prerequisiteO(V + E)
Dijkstraa vertex popped with its smallest distance is final (no negative edges)O((V + E) log V): E pushes, each log V
Bellman–Fordafter round r, dist ≤ the best path with at most r edgesO(V·E): V − 1 rounds over E edges
Kruskalthe kept edges form a forest inside some MSTO(E log E) for the sort
DP tableeach cell holds the answer to its subproblem, filled after its dependenciescells × work per cell
A model answer: “Explain Dijkstra”

“Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source when no edge is negative. I keep a min-heap of (distance, vertex). I pop the smallest; if it is stale I skip it; otherwise its distance is final, because any other route must go through a vertex still in the heap whose distance is at least as large, and edges cannot make it smaller. I then relax its edges and push improvements. Each edge causes at most one push, so the cost is O((V + E) log V). I would test an unreachable vertex, a graph with one vertex, and two equal-length paths. With a negative edge the finality claim breaks, so I would use Bellman–Ford.”

Foundations line · merge sort, amortised analysis, hashing, what comes next

Appendix: beyond the outline

Big idea

Beyond the course outline. Everything here is optional for the end-sem. These are the topics a strong algorithms course would add next: merge sort and counting inversions during the merge, amortised analysis (why occasional expensive steps average out), and hashing (what a Python dict does underneath). They explain costs you have been quoting without proof, such as union-find and heap-build. A final page lists what comes after, with pointers, so you know it exists.

1. Merge sort

Quick Sort (stop 3) partitions then recurses. Merge sort recurses then merges: split the list in half, sort each half, merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. Every level of the recursion does O(n) merging and there are log₂ n levels, so the cost is O(n log n) in every case, with no bad input. The price is O(n) extra space for the merge.

It is stable: items that compare equal keep their original order, as long as ties are resolved in favour of the left half (<=, not <). Python’s built-in sort is stable too, which is why sorting by one key and then another works.

Hand trace of the merge of [2, 5, 9] and [3, 4, 10]: compare 2 and 3, take 2; 5 and 3, take 3; 5 and 4, take 4; 5 and 10, take 5; 9 and 10, take 9; the left side is empty, so append the rest: [2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10].

The contest payoff: counting while you merge

An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]. During a merge, when you take an item from the right half while left items remain, that right item is smaller than all of them: you have just counted that many inversions in O(1). This turns the O(n²) pair count into O(n log n). The same idea answers LC 315 (for each element, how many later elements are smaller; sort the indices so you remember who is who) and LC 493 (count pairs with a[i] > 2·a[j] in a separate sweep before each merge, since both halves are sorted). Stop 2 uses merge sort to show the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), and the sorting patterns in stop 3 have a plain count_inversions; LC 912 itself is simply “implement a sort”.

Practice

LC 912, LC 315, LC 493 (all on the Ladder, tab Sorting). Checked against the O(n²) pair count and, for stability, against Python’s stable sorted.

2. Amortised analysis

Some operations are usually cheap and occasionally expensive. Amortised cost is the average per operation over a whole sequence, worst case guaranteed. It is not average over random inputs.

The dynamic array. list.append is O(1) most of the time, but when the array is full it allocates a bigger one and copies everything. If the capacity doubles, the copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, …, and the sum of that series is less than 2n. So n appends cost under 3n elementary steps in total: O(1) amortised per append. If the capacity grew by only 1 each time, the copies would be 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2, which is O(n²). The multiplicative growth is what matters.

The code counts the copies: after n appends with doubling, copies < 2n; with growth by one it is exactly n(n − 1)/2 (both asserted for sizes up to 5,000).

Other costs you have been quoting. Building a heap from n items is O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a step or two (stop 5). Union-find with union by size and path compression costs O(α(n)) amortised per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any input that fits in a computer; that is why Kruskal’s sort dominates its running time. Monotonic stacks are O(n) because each element is pushed once and popped at most once, however many pops one step makes. All three use the same accounting idea: a charge per item, paid once.

3. Hashing, and what a dict does

A hash table stores a key at position hash(key) % size. Two keys can land on the same position: a collision. There are two standard answers.

  • Chaining. Each position holds a small list of the entries that landed there. Lookup walks one list. Simple, and deletes are easy.
  • Open addressing. One entry per slot; on a collision, probe the next slot (linear probing: the next one, then the next…). A deleted slot must become a tombstone, not empty: an empty slot ends a search, and would cut off the keys that were placed after it.

The load factor is entries ÷ slots. As it rises, chains lengthen and probe runs grow, so tables resize (usually doubling) and re-place every key, which is another amortised O(1) argument. With a good hash and a controlled load factor, insert, lookup and delete cost O(1) on average. The worst case is O(n), if every key collides. This is why Python’s dict and set are fast but can be slowed by an adversarial input in a contest, and why keys must be hashable (a list is not; use a tuple).

Both maps were run against Python’s own dict on random sequences of inserts, updates, lookups and deletes with integer and string keys, and the load factor stayed below its limit.

LC 146 LRU Cache is a hash table plus a doubly linked list: the table finds an entry in O(1), the list moves it to the front in O(1), and the back of the list is always the least recently used. Sentinel nodes at both ends remove the edge cases. LC 705 and LC 706 ask you to build a set and a map from nothing; fixed-size chaining, as in MyHashMap, is enough.

Practice

LC 146, LC 705, LC 706 (Ladder tab Arrays and search). The LRU cache was checked against Python’s OrderedDict on random operation sequences.

The Vault: problems that don’t look like anything you’ve seen

Chakravyuh was hard because the pattern was new, not because the code was long. These six problems are written the same way: a plain statement, two subtasks, and one observation between you and the full marks. Each follows the routine of stop 14: read the subtasks, write the brute force, then look for the trick. Every solution below was checked against its brute force on thousands of random inputs. The Ladder’s Vault tab adds real Codeforces problems chosen for the same quality, grouped by the trick.

≈ CF 1900 · graphs · subtasks 40 / 60

Chakravyuh Reversed

Every node of a directed graph on nodes 0 … n−1 has at most one outgoing edge. You are told, for every node i, the number c[i] of distinct nodes reachable from i by following edges as long as possible, counting i itself. Print any array a (a[i] = −1 for no edge, otherwise the node i points to) that produces exactly this c, or print −1 if no graph does.

Subtask 1: n ≤ 6. Subtask 2: n ≤ 10⁵, 1 ≤ c[i] ≤ n.

Hints (one at a time)

1. What value does a node on a cycle of length L have? What value does a node hanging off one of them have, compared with its successor?

2. Count how many nodes hold each value v.

3. A node with value v ≥ 2 either points to a node with value v − 1, or lies on a cycle of exactly v nodes.

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick and the full solution

Group nodes by value. Value 1: dead ends. Value v ≥ 2: if any node has value v − 1, point every v-node at it; otherwise the v-nodes must form cycles of length v, so their count must be a multiple of v. The solution is reverse_chak in stop 8; it matched every possible graph for n ≤ 5.

≈ CF 1700 · graphs · subtasks 30 / 70

Odd Walk

A country has n cities and m two-way roads. Find the fewest roads in a trip from city s to city t that uses an odd number of roads. A trip may use the same road, or visit the same city, any number of times. Print −1 if no such trip exists.

Subtask 1: n ≤ 8. Subtask 2: n, m ≤ 2·10⁵.

Hints

1. A city can be reached by both an odd and an even trip. Do they need the same distance?

2. What if each city had two distances?

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick and the full solution

The node is (city, parity of roads so far). Every road flips the parity, so a plain BFS over these doubled nodes finds the shortest odd trip. See shortest_odd_walk in stop 8.

≈ CF 1900 · graphs II · subtasks 30 / 70

Free Passes

n cities, m one-way roads with non-negative tolls. You hold k passes; each pass makes one road on your route free. What is the cheapest trip from city 0 to city n−1? Print −1 if there is no route.

Subtask 1: n ≤ 6, k ≤ 3. Subtask 2: n ≤ 10⁵, m ≤ 2·10⁵, k ≤ 10.

Hints

1. Where would you remember how many passes are left?

2. Draw k + 1 copies of the map. What does using a pass look like as an edge?

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick and the full solution

Dijkstra on states (city, passes used): a normal edge stays in the same layer at its toll, a pass edge goes one layer down at cost 0. The answer is the best over all layers of city n−1. See min_cost_k_free in stop 12.

≈ CF 1800 · monotonic stack · subtasks 40 / 60

Visible Pairs

n people stand in a row with heights h[i]. Two people i < j can see each other when nobody standing between them is taller than the shorter of the two. Count the pairs that can see each other.

Subtask 1: n ≤ 3,000. Subtask 2: n ≤ 2·10⁵, heights up to 10⁹, and equal heights do occur.

Hints

1. For person j, which earlier people can still see them? Think of the people who haven’t been blocked yet.

2. Keep them in a stack in order of height. When j arrives, who gets popped, and why do they never matter again?

3. What do you store so equal heights are counted correctly?

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick and the full solution

Monotonic stack of (height, count). Everyone shorter than the newcomer is popped and sees them once; then the newcomer sees the equal group, and the first taller person behind it. See visible_pairs in stop 13.

≈ CF 2000 · backtracking · subtasks 40 / 60

Split the Treasure

You found n gems with integer values (some are cursed and negative). Count the subsets of gems whose values add up to exactly T. The empty subset counts if T = 0. Two subsets are different if they use different gems, even when the values are equal.

Subtask 1: n ≤ 20. Subtask 2: n ≤ 36.

Hints

1. 2³⁶ is far too many; 2¹⁸ is not.

2. List all subset sums of each half separately.

3. A subset is a left part plus a right part. For a left sum s, how many right parts sum to T − s?

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick and the full solution

Meet in the middle: count the left half’s sums in a dictionary and look up T − s for every right-half sum. See count_subsets in stop 6.

≈ CF 1700 · observation · subtasks 30 / 70

Frozen Middle

A row of n cards holds a permutation of 0 … n−1. You may swap the cards at positions i and j only when |i − j| ≥ k. Using any number of legal swaps, can you sort the row into 0, 1, …, n−1?

Subtask 1: n ≤ 7. Subtask 2: n ≤ 2·10⁵.

Hints

1. Write the BFS for n ≤ 7 and print which rows are sortable for n = 5, k = 3. Look at what the unsortable ones have in common.

2. Which positions have no legal partner at all, whatever the other cards do?

Subtask 1: the brute force
The trick

Position i can swap with j ≤ i − k or j ≥ i + k. Positions n − k … k − 1 have neither, so they are frozen: those cards must already be correct. Everything else is movable enough to be sorted. The one-line check sortable above matches the brute force on every permutation with n ≤ 6 and every k. Why the rest is always fixable is worth proving yourself.

Timed mocks

Three-rung mocks use real Codeforces problems at the exam’s 1400, 1500 and 1600, the Summit mocks one tier above, the Ego mocks two. Open all three problems, press Start, and score honestly: nothing, a brute force that passed some tests, or fully accepted.

Your end-sem is LeetCode-style, so here are three-problem LeetCode mocks, one easy, one medium and one hard, built from the topics of stops 9–17. Mark a brute force that passes some tests as half; the clock decides how much of each you can finish.

The original LeetCode-style mocks A–H, four problems each, are still here:

After every mock
  • For each problem not fully accepted, write one line: the pattern, and the twist you missed.
  • For each zero, write the brute force now, untimed. If it takes under ten minutes, the zero was a routine failure, not a knowledge gap.
  • Read the idea, close it, and re-code the problem from a blank file the next day.
  • Say three sentences out loud for every problem you solved: the pattern, the state or observation, the complexity. That is the Mock AI Interview (10%).

Exam-style practice problems

How to practise

Write each answer on paper, the way you would in the exam: a table for every dry run, the recurrence before the answer, the five DP questions before any code. Try for 10 minutes before opening the hint, and 10 more before the solution. Reading a solution feels like understanding; producing it from a blank page is what the exam asks for. Problems follow the order of the stops.

Problem 1: complexity of code

Count the work in three functions

Give the time complexity of each function in Θ notation, with a one-line justification, and the space complexity of c.

Hint

For a, write down how many times the inner loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, … and add them up. For b, ask how many halvings reach 1. For c, write the recurrence first: how many recursive calls, on what size, plus how much other work?

Solution

a: the inner loop runs n − i times, so the total is n + (n − 1) + … + 1 = n(n + 1)/2. That is Θ(n²). Space O(1).

b: i is halved each pass, so the loop runs about log₂ n times: Θ(log n).

c: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1). Master theorem: a = 2, b = 2, c = log₂ 2 = 1. f(n) = 1 is polynomially smaller than n¹, so the leaves dominate: Θ(n). (Calling c(n // 2) twice doubles the number of calls at every level, so the recursion tree ends with about n leaves. One call would give Θ(log n).) Space: the recursion goes log₂ n levels deep, so O(log n) stack.

Problem 2: recurrences

Solve four recurrences with the Master theorem

For each, state a, b, c = log_b(a), which case applies and the answer. If the theorem does not apply, say why and solve it another way.

(i) T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n   (ii) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n   (iii) T(n) = T(n/2) + n   (iv) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n

Hint

Compare f(n) with n^c. Smaller by a power of n: leaves win. Equal: every level is equal, multiply by log n. Larger by a power of n (and the regularity check holds): the root wins. Bigger by only a log factor is the gap.

Solution
a, bc = log_b af(n) vs n^cAnswer
(i)4, 22n is polynomially smaller than n²Θ(n²)
(ii)2, 21n = Θ(n¹): equalΘ(n log n)
(iii)1, 20n is polynomially larger than n⁰ = 1; regularity: 1 · (n/2) ≤ ½ · n holdsΘ(n)
(iv)2, 21n log n is larger than n, but only by a log factor, not by any n^εTheorem does not apply

For (iv), draw the recursion tree. Level k has 2ᵏ subproblems of size n/2ᵏ, each costing (n/2ᵏ) log(n/2ᵏ), so level k costs n(log n − k). Adding over log n levels gives about n · (log n)²/2, so T(n) = Θ(n log² n).

Problem 3: Quick Sort dry run

Partition [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3], then finish the sort

Use the last element as the pivot (Lomuto). Show the array and k after every step of the first partition, then list every later call to partition and count the comparisons in total.

Hint

k starts at lo − 1 = −1. Each time arr[pos] ≤ pivot, add one to k and swap arr[k] with arr[pos]. At the end the pivot swaps into k + 1. A partition of a range with m elements makes m − 1 comparisons.

Solution
posarr[pos] ≤ 3?kArray after the step
start−1[5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3]
05: no−1[5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3]
12: yes, swap arr[0] and arr[1]0[2, 5, 8, 1, 9, 3]
28: no0[2, 5, 8, 1, 9, 3]
31: yes, swap arr[1] and arr[3]1[2, 1, 8, 5, 9, 3]
49: no1[2, 1, 8, 5, 9, 3]
endpivot into k + 1 = 21[2, 1, 3, 5, 9, 8], returns 2

Next calls: partition(arr, 0, 1) on [2, 1] with pivot 1 gives [1, 2], pivot at index 0. partition(arr, 3, 5) on [5, 9, 8] with pivot 8 gives [5, 8, 9], pivot at index 4. Every remaining range has 0 or 1 element. Final array [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9].

Comparisons: 5 + 1 + 2 = 8. A sorted input of the same size would cost 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15, the worst case.

Problem 4: BST operations

Build, traverse, delete

Insert 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30 into an empty BST in that order. Draw it, give its height in edges, and write the inorder, preorder and postorder traversals. Then delete 25 and give the new preorder and height.

Hint

Each key walks down from the root: smaller goes left, larger goes right, until an empty spot. 25 has two children, so replace it with its inorder successor: the smallest key in its right subtree.

Solution

Shape: 45 has children 25 and 65; 25 has 15 and 35; 35 has a left child 30; 65 has 55 and 75. The longest root-to-leaf path is 45 → 25 → 35 → 30, so the height is 3.

TraversalBeforeAfter deleting 25
Inorder15 25 30 35 45 55 65 7515 30 35 45 55 65 75
Preorder45 25 15 35 30 65 55 7545 30 15 35 65 55 75
Postorder15 30 35 25 55 75 65 4515 35 30 55 75 65 45

Delete 25: the successor is the minimum of the right subtree (35 → 30), so 30 is copied into 25's node and the old 30 leaf is removed. 35 is left with no children and the height drops to 2. The inorder list is still sorted, which is how you check your answer.

Problem 5: heaps

Build a max-heap from [4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 8], then delete the max

Use the O(n) bottom-up method. Show the array after every sift_down call, then show the array after one delete_max.

Hint

n = 6, so the last parent is at index n // 2 − 1 = 2. Sift down index 2, then 1, then 0. Each sift down swaps with the larger child and keeps going until the order rule holds.

Solution
StepWhat happensArray
start[4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 8]
sift_down(2)3 vs its only child 8: swap[4, 10, 8, 5, 1, 3]
sift_down(1)10 vs children 5 and 1: already fine[4, 10, 8, 5, 1, 3]
sift_down(0)4 vs 10 and 8: swap with 10; then 4 vs 5 and 1: swap with 5[10, 5, 8, 4, 1, 3]
delete_maxreturn 10; last value 3 moves to the root; 3 vs 5 and 8: swap with 8; index 2 has no children[8, 5, 3, 4, 1]

Check: every parent is at least as large as its children (8 ≥ 5, 3; 5 ≥ 4, 1). Building cost O(n), the delete O(log n).

Problem 6: backtracking

Subsets that add up to a target

Write a backtracking function that returns every subset of a list of distinct positive integers whose sum equals a target, using each number at most once. Prune as early as you can. Give the output for nums = [2, 3, 5, 6], target = 8, and the worst-case time.

Hint

Sort the list first. The state is (start index, remaining sum). If the next number is bigger than what remains, every number after it is too, so you can stop the loop.

Solution

Worst case every subset is explored: O(2ⁿ) nodes, O(n · 2ⁿ) counting the copies. The sort costs O(n log n) once and makes the break prune whole branches.

Problem 7: graph traversal

DFS, BFS and shortest paths by hand

An undirected graph has 6 vertices and edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5. Write the adjacency list (neighbours in increasing order). Starting from 0, give the DFS visit order, the BFS order, the BFS distance of every vertex and the shortest path from 0 to 5. Does the graph have a cycle?

Hint

DFS: go as deep as possible through the smallest unvisited neighbour, back out only when stuck. BFS: process the queue in order, marking each vertex as it is enqueued. Keep a parent array to rebuild the path.

Solution

Adjacency list: 0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 3], 2: [0, 3], 3: [1, 2, 4], 4: [3, 5], 5: [4].

QuestionAnswer
DFS order0 1 3 2 4 5
BFS order0 1 2 3 4 5
BFS distances (vertex 0 to 5)0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4
Parents1 ← 0, 2 ← 0, 3 ← 1, 4 ← 3, 5 ← 4
Shortest path 0 to 50 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 5 (4 edges)

Cycle: yes, 0 – 1 – 3 – 2 – 0. DFS finds it when, at vertex 2, it sees 0 already visited and 0 is not 2's parent. One connected component; degree sum 12 = 2 × 6 edges. Both traversals are O(V + E).

Problem 8: dynamic programming in one dimension

Fewest coins

Coins come in values 1, 3 and 4 (as many of each as you like). Find the fewest coins that make 6. Answer the five DP questions, fill the table, write the code and give its complexity. Why does greedy fail here?

Hint

State: dp[a] = fewest coins that make amount a. Choice: which coin is used last. If the last coin is c, the rest makes a − c.

Solution

State dp[a]: fewest coins for amount a. Choices: the last coin c. Transition: dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c ≤ a of dp[a − c]. Base: dp[0] = 0. Order: a from 1 up to the amount; the answer is dp[6].

a0123456
dp[a]0121122

Answer: 2 coins (3 + 3). Greedy grabs the biggest coin first: 4 + 1 + 1, which is 3 coins. Time O(amount × number of coins), space O(amount).

Problem 9: dynamic programming in two dimensions

0/1 Knapsack table and traceback

Items have weights [1, 3, 4, 5] and values [1, 4, 5, 7]; the capacity is 7. Fill the table dp[i][c] (best value using the first i items with capacity c), give the best value and which items achieve it.

Hint

Row 0 is all zeros. For each cell: skip item i (copy the cell above) or, if it fits, take it (value plus the cell one row up and w columns left). Trace back from the bottom-right: if a cell differs from the one above, the item was taken.

Solution
i (w, v)c = 01234567
0 (none)00000000
1 (1, 1)01111111
2 (3, 4)01145555
3 (4, 5)01145669
4 (5, 7)01145789

Best value 9. Traceback from dp[4][7] = 9: equal to dp[3][7], so item 4 is skipped. dp[3][7] = 9 differs from dp[2][7] = 5, so item 3 (weight 4) is taken; move to c = 3. dp[2][3] = 4 differs from dp[1][3] = 1, so item 2 (weight 3) is taken; c = 0. Items 2 and 3: weight 7, value 9. Time and space O(nW).

Master theorem on one card

T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)        let c = log_b(a)      compare f(n) with n^c

f(n) polynomially smaller than n^c  →  T(n) = Θ(n^c)            leaves dominate
f(n) = Θ(n^c)                       →  T(n) = Θ(n^c · log n)    every level equal
f(n) polynomially larger than n^c   →  T(n) = Θ(f(n))           root dominates
                                        (and a·f(n/b) ≤ k·f(n), k < 1)
Gap (e.g. f = n^c · log n): theorem fails. Use a recursion tree.

Data structure rule cards

BST

Left < node < right at every node. Inorder is sorted. Cost O(h). Delete: leaf, one child, or two children (replace with inorder successor).

Heap

Complete tree + parent ≥ children (max). Array: children 2i+1, 2i+2; parent (i−1)//2. Insert = bubble up. Delete = swap root with last, sift down. Build = O(n).

Backtracking

Choose, explore, undo. Prune early. Copy before saving. Counts: n! permutations, 2ⁿ subsets.

Graph

Adjacency list for sparse graphs: O(V+E). Matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge test. Sum of degrees = 2E.

DFS / BFS

visited[] always. DFS = stack/recursion, finds cycles and components. BFS = queue, mark when enqueued, shortest path in unweighted graphs.

DP

State, choices, transition, base, order. Memo = recursion + cache. Naive Fibonacci-type recursion is exponential, DP makes it linear.

2D DP

State is a pair (i, j). Time = cells × work per cell. LCS: match → diagonal + 1, else max(up, left). Knapsack: max(skip, take); 1D version loops capacity downward. Keep the full table if you need the traceback.

Exam-writing tips

  • For "analyse the complexity", name the recurrence or the loop count first, then simplify. Marks are for the working.
  • For "dry run", draw a table with one row per step. Show the state after every step (array, stack, queue, visited).
  • State your assumptions: index base (0 or 1), duplicate policy, tree height convention, adjacency order.
  • Always say which case you are discussing: best, average or worst.
Added: missing from your notes

Corrections and clarifications to your lecture notes, collected in one place:
(1) BST operations are O(h), not O(log n), unless the tree is balanced. (2) The row "2T(n/2)+O(1) → BST ops → O(n)" in the quick-reference table really describes a full traversal. (3) Quick Sort's O(log n) space is an average; worst case O(n) unless you recurse into the smaller side first. (4) The notes' Master theorem has no "polynomially" or regularity condition; the gap case n log n exists. (5) DFS/BFS time O(V+E) assumes adjacency lists. (6) Heap build is O(n), not O(n log n). (7) Heap delete swaps with the larger child.

Model structure for long-answer questions

Question typeWhat to write, in order
"Explain algorithm X with an example"1. One-sentence idea. 2. Steps or pseudocode. 3. A small worked example as a table, state after every step. 4. Time and space complexity (best, average, worst). 5. One strength and one weakness.
"State and explain the rules of data structure Y"1. Definition. 2. Shape rule and order rule, with a small valid and invalid example. 3. How it is stored. 4. Each operation with cost. 5. When to use it.
"Analyse the complexity of this code / recurrence"1. Say what n is. 2. Count (loops multiply, sequence adds) or write the recurrence. 3. Solve (recursion tree or Master theorem, showing a, b, c and the case). 4. State Θ or O, and space.
"Compare X and Y"A table with the same rows for both: idea, time (best/avg/worst), space, when to prefer each.
"Trace / dry run"Table with one row per step; columns for the variables, data structure contents, and output so far.
"Design a solution for problem Z"Brute force and its cost, the observation that improves it, the chosen technique, pseudocode, dry run on the example, complexity.

Bridge essentials

Half stopMust-know
0.5Trace one row per step. Code after a recursive call runs on the way back. Deepest stack = recursion space.
1.5f/g → 0: slower; → constant: Θ; → ∞: faster. logs < powers < exponentials < factorials. 4ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ). Induction: base, assume k, prove k + 1.
2.5Reader–writer partition: k ends the kept zone; grow k, then swap. Not stable. Three-way partition for duplicates.
3.5Mutating is shared, rebinding is local. Return and re-attach subtrees. Save nxt before turning an arrow.
4.50-based: children 2i + 1, 2i + 2; parent (i − 1) // 2. Height ⌊log₂ n⌋, leaves from index n // 2.
5.5kⁿ, 2ⁿ, n!, n!/(n − k)!, C(n, k). Brute force: 2ⁿ to n ≈ 25, n! to n ≈ 11. Record cur[:].
6.5At most n(n − 1)/2 undirected edges. [[0] * C for _ in range(R)]. Grid cell: up to 4 neighbours.
7.5Queue → BFS, stack → deep first. Visited set because of cycles. O(V + E).
8.5DP needs overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. lru_cache needs hashable arguments. Greedy needs a proof.
9.5Table (m + 1) × (n + 1); dp[i][j] compares x[i − 1] and y[j − 1]; fill so sources come first.
10.5Counting is not listing. Fewest equal-cost steps → BFS. Best or count over overlapping choices → DP.
During the exam
  • Read every question first and note what each one asks for: a trace, a complexity argument, code, or a comparison.
  • For a dry run, draw the table before you start: one row per step, the whole state in every row.
  • Write the loop count or the recurrence before the answer. The working earns most of the marks.
  • Before handing in, scan for: 0-based indices, < versus <=, the pivot left out of both halves, the larger child in sift down, a copy before saving in backtracking, marking on enqueue in BFS.
